START HERE

Practise English every day

The best websites for each IELTS skill – the top 5 are free

Lessons alone are not enough to reach Band 6–8: you need a little practice every day. These pages list the 7 best websites for each skill. Numbers 1–5 are free; 6 and 7 are excellent paid options if you want more.

Thời gian học trên lớp là chưa đủ để đạt Band 6–8 – bạn cần luyện tập một chút mỗi ngày. Các trang dưới đây giới thiệu 7 trang web tốt nhất cho từng kỹ năng: số 1–5 miễn phí, số 6 và 7 là lựa chọn trả phí nếu bạn muốn học thêm.

Choose a skill
ListeningTop pick: IELTS.org – Official sample tests (Listening)
ReadingTop pick: British Council – Free IELTS Academic Reading practice tests
WritingTop pick: Write & Improve (Cambridge)
SpeakingTop pick: Speak & Improve (Cambridge)
A simple plan (20–30 minutes a day)
  • Every day: 10 minutes of listening and 10 minutes of reading.
  • Three times a week: 10 minutes of speaking – record yourself and listen back.
  • Once or twice a week: write one Task 1 or Task 2 answer and check it with a free writing tool.

chapters.label: Listening websites
chapters.html:
LISTENING

The 7 best websites for listening

Numbers 1–5 are free · 6 and 7 are paid options

Pick one or two websites and use them a little every day – that works better than trying them all once. Links open in a new tab.

1  IELTS.org – Official sample tests (Listening)FreeBand 5+ (free, no account needed)

The official IELTS website's free sample tasks for every Listening question type, plus a full practice test in the computer format.

Why it helps for IELTS: These are real materials from the test makers, with answer keys and transcripts, in the on-screen format IELTS Academic now uses.

How to use it: Do one question type a day, check the answer key, then listen again with the transcript to see exactly why each wrong answer was wrong.

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày làm một dạng câu hỏi, đối chiếu đáp án, rồi nghe lại kèm transcript để hiểu vì sao mình chọn sai.

2  British Council – IELTS Ready (free account)FreeBand 5+ (free account; Premium (40 tests) only if you book your test with the British Council)

The British Council's official IELTS practice platform, where a free account gives a mini mock test with AI feedback, two full mock tests with scores and short skills courses.

Why it helps for IELTS: Timed full mock tests with Listening scores and model answers show students their real band before test day.

How to use it: Take the first full mock test at the start and the second near the end of the course, then compare your Listening scores.

Gợi ý: Tạo tài khoản miễn phí, làm một bài thi thử đầy đủ ngay tuần đầu và bài thứ hai gần cuối khóa để so sánh điểm Listening.

3  BBC Learning English – 6 Minute EnglishFreeBand 5+ (free, no account needed)

A weekly six-minute programme in which two BBC presenters discuss a topical question, with a free transcript, vocabulary list and downloadable audio.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its topics (health, technology, environment, society) match IELTS Listening Parts 3–4 and Speaking Part 3, and the transcript lets students check every word.

How to use it: Do one episode a day: listen once without the transcript, then read along and note five new phrases.

Website does not open on your internet? Use BBC Learning English on YouTube instead (same lessons).

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày nghe một tập: lần đầu không xem transcript, lần sau vừa nghe vừa đọc và ghi lại 5 cụm từ mới.

4  British Council LearnEnglish – ListeningFreeB1–C1 (about Band 4–8) (free, no account needed)

Graded listening lessons from A1 to C1, such as lectures, interviews and podcasts, each with a preparation task, two comprehension tasks and a transcript.

Why it helps for IELTS: B2–C1 lessons like 'A lecture about an experiment' train the note-taking and detail-spotting that IELTS Parts 3–4 demand.

How to use it: Start at B1 or B2, do both tasks first, then open the Transcript tab to find what you missed.

Gợi ý: Chọn bài ở trình độ B1 hoặc B2, làm bài tập trước rồi mở tab Transcript để xem mình nghe sót chỗ nào.

5  TED TalksFreeBand 6+ (free, no account needed)

Thousands of short talks by experts on science, education, technology and society, with interactive transcripts and subtitles in many languages, including Vietnamese.

Why it helps for IELTS: A TED talk is very close to the academic monologue of IELTS Listening Part 4 and builds topic vocabulary for Writing and Speaking.

How to use it: Choose a talk under 10 minutes, watch with English subtitles, then watch again without them and summarise the main points in three sentences.

Gợi ý: Chọn bài nói dưới 10 phút, xem với phụ đề tiếng Anh, rồi xem lại không phụ đề và tóm tắt ý chính bằng 3 câu.

Paid options – only if you want more

Very good, but they cost money. The free websites above are enough to reach your target band.

6  ELLLO (English Listening Lesson Library Online)Freeall levels (A2–C1) (free, no account needed)

Over 3,000 short listening lessons with real speakers from many countries, each with audio or video, a transcript, vocabulary notes and a quiz.

Why it helps for IELTS: IELTS recordings use a range of accents, and ELLLO's natural conversations train students to follow different speakers.

How to use it: Do one lesson a day at your level, take the quiz, then shadow three sentences from the transcript aloud.

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày học một bài đúng trình độ, làm quiz rồi đọc theo (shadowing) 3 câu trong transcript để quen nhiều giọng khác nhau.

7  Cambridge IELTS 21 Academic (official practice tests)PaidBand 5.5+ (book with audio, about £39 in the UK – buy an official copy)

Cambridge's newest book (July 2026) of four authentic IELTS Academic papers, with Listening audio, answers, sample Writing answers and an example Speaking video.

Why it helps for IELTS: These are genuine past papers from the test makers, the most accurate full-test practice there is for Listening and Reading.

How to use it: Do one full test every two weeks under timed conditions, then study every wrong answer with the transcript.

Gợi ý: Nên mua sách bản quyền, cứ hai tuần làm một đề đầy đủ có bấm giờ, sau đó xem lại kỹ từng câu sai.

chapters.label: Reading websites
chapters.html:
READING

The 7 best websites for reading

Numbers 1–5 are free · 6 and 7 are paid options

Pick one or two websites and use them a little every day – that works better than trying them all once. Links open in a new tab.

1  British Council – Free IELTS Academic Reading practice testsFreeBand 5+ (free, no account needed)

Official sample tasks with answer keys for every Academic Reading question type, a full three-passage computer practice test and printable paper samples.

Why it helps for IELTS: The British Council says these tests use real IELTS questions from past papers, so students practise exactly the True/False/Not Given, headings and completion tasks of the exam.

How to use it: Practise one question type at a time, then do the full 60-minute test on a computer to get used to the real screen.

Gợi ý: Luyện từng dạng câu hỏi trước, sau đó làm trọn bài 60 phút trên máy tính để quen thao tác như khi thi thật.

2  The ConversationFreeBand 6+ (free, no paywall)

A news site where university researchers write short, clearly edited articles about their own fields.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its academic-but-readable articles on science, health, education and the environment read very much like IELTS Academic passages.

How to use it: Read one article a day, write a one-line summary of each paragraph (like Matching Headings) and save five academic words.

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày đọc một bài, tóm tắt mỗi đoạn bằng một câu (giống dạng Matching Headings) và ghi lại 5 từ học thuật.

3  Breaking News EnglishFreeall levels (A1–C1) (free, no account needed)

Current news stories rewritten at seven levels (0–6), each with audio and many printable exercises.

Why it helps for IELTS: Reading the same story at a harder level each time builds the speed and vocabulary needed for long IELTS passages.

How to use it: Read a story at your level, then read it again one level higher and do the gap-fill and true/false exercises.

Gợi ý: Đọc một bài ở trình độ hiện tại, sau đó đọc bản khó hơn một bậc và làm bài điền từ, đúng/sai.

4  The GuardianFreeBand 6.5+ (free, no paywall)

A leading British newspaper whose high-quality reporting, including science, environment, education and long-read features, is free online.

Why it helps for IELTS: Authentic, well-edited articles on typical IELTS topics help Band 6.5+ students read faster and meet advanced vocabulary in context.

How to use it: Read one Science or Environment article a day and underline the sentences that show the writer's opinion, as practice for Yes/No/Not Given.

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày đọc một bài mục Science hoặc Environment và gạch chân những câu nêu quan điểm của tác giả để luyện dạng Yes/No/Not Given.

5  Cambridge Dictionary (English–Vietnamese)Freeall levels (free; a free +Plus account adds word lists and quizzes)

Cambridge's learner dictionary with clear English definitions, UK/US pronunciation, real example sentences and an English–Vietnamese dictionary.

Why it helps for IELTS: Learner definitions plus Vietnamese translations let students understand academic words quickly and save them for review.

How to use it: Look up only the key words you meet while reading, add them to a +Plus word list and test yourself with its quiz each week.

Gợi ý: Chỉ tra những từ then chốt khi đọc, lưu vào word list trên Cambridge +Plus và ôn lại bằng quiz mỗi tuần.

Paid options – only if you want more

Very good, but they cost money. The free websites above are enough to reach your target band.

6  Exam English – IELTS Academic Reading testsFreeBand 5.5+ (free, no account needed)

Ten free IELTS-style Academic Reading passages with questions you can check online, from a long-running exam-practice site.

Why it helps for IELTS: Extra full-length passages with IELTS question types give more timed practice once the official samples are finished.

How to use it: Give yourself 20 minutes per passage, as in the real test, and write down why each wrong answer was wrong.

Gợi ý: Làm mỗi bài trong 20 phút như thi thật và ghi lại lý do sai cho từng câu.

7  The EconomistPaidBand 7+ (1-month free trial, then about US$47 a month)

A world-famous weekly magazine on economics, politics, science and technology, known for dense, precise writing.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its style is close to the hardest IELTS Reading passages and gives Band 7+ students models of advanced argument.

How to use it: During the free trial, read one Science & technology article a day and paraphrase its main claim in your own words.

Gợi ý: Tận dụng tháng dùng thử miễn phí: mỗi ngày đọc một bài mục Science & technology và diễn đạt lại ý chính bằng lời của mình.

chapters.label: Writing websites
chapters.html:
WRITING

The 7 best websites for writing

Numbers 1–5 are free · 6 and 7 are paid options

Pick one or two websites and use them a little every day – that works better than trying them all once. Links open in a new tab.

1  Write & Improve (Cambridge)Free (paid extras)Band 5+ (free; IELTS Test Zone £4.50/month, 10 IELTS tasks free)

Cambridge's free online tool that marks your writing in seconds and highlights the words and sentences to improve.

Why it helps for IELTS: Students can rewrite and resubmit until their level rises, and the IELTS Test Zone gives band scores on realistic Task 1 and Task 2 questions.

How to use it: Write a Task 2 essay, submit it, fix the highlighted parts and resubmit until the score stops rising.

Gợi ý: Viết bài, nộp để hệ thống chấm, sửa những chỗ được tô màu rồi nộp lại cho đến khi điểm không tăng nữa.

2  IELTS.org – Writing test resourcesFreeBand 5.5+ (free, no account needed)

Official videos explaining how examiners mark IELTS Writing, plus the band descriptors and sample answers with examiner comments.

Why it helps for IELTS: Knowing the four marking criteria (Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammar) shows students exactly what lifts a 6 to a 7.

How to use it: Watch one video a week, then mark your own essay against the band descriptors before a teacher marks it.

Gợi ý: Mỗi tuần xem một video, rồi tự chấm bài của mình theo band descriptors trước khi nộp cho giáo viên.

3  IELTS Liz – Writing Task 1 & Task 2Free (paid extras)Band 5.5+ (free; optional paid lessons)

A long-running free IELTS site by an experienced teacher, with tips, over 100 essay questions and band 9 model answers for both writing tasks.

Why it helps for IELTS: Her model essays and planning tips show students how to write clear, well-organised answers for every Task 2 essay type.

How to use it: Write your own essay on one of her questions first, then compare it with her model and borrow structures, not sentences.

Gợi ý: Tự viết bài theo đề của Liz trước, sau đó so với bài mẫu để học cách triển khai ý, không chép nguyên câu.

4  IELTS Advantage – free Writing guidesFree (paid extras)Band 5+ (free articles and videos; paid course)

Free step-by-step guides, videos and sample answers for Writing Task 1 and Task 2 from a large online IELTS school.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its five-step Task 2 method (understand the question, plan, introduction, body, conclusion) gives Band 5–6 students a reliable structure.

How to use it: Write one essay a week with the five steps and spend the first 10 minutes only analysing the question and planning.

Gợi ý: Mỗi tuần viết một bài theo 5 bước của IELTS Advantage và dành 10 phút đầu chỉ để phân tích đề và lập dàn ý.

5  Academic Phrasebank (University of Manchester)FreeBand 6+ (free website)

A free bank of academic phrases organised by function, such as comparing, explaining causes, giving examples and describing trends.

Why it helps for IELTS: Ready-made phrases for comparing, cause and effect and trends improve Coherence and Lexical Resource in both Writing tasks.

How to use it: Before each essay, choose three phrases from 'Explaining causality' or 'Describing trends' and use them correctly.

Gợi ý: Trước mỗi bài viết, chọn 3 cụm từ trong mục 'Explaining causality' hoặc 'Describing trends' và dùng đúng ngữ cảnh.

Paid options – only if you want more

Very good, but they cost money. The free websites above are enough to reach your target band.

6  Grammarly (free version)Free (paid extras)Band 5+ (free account; Pro about US$12 a month)

A writing assistant that flags spelling, grammar and punctuation mistakes as you type in the browser, Word or Google Docs.

Why it helps for IELTS: Seeing the same grammar and spelling errors flagged again and again helps students raise their Grammatical Range and Accuracy score.

How to use it: Write the essay yourself first, then run Grammarly and copy each mistake into an error log; never let AI rewrite your essay.

Gợi ý: Tự viết xong rồi mới dùng Grammarly để soát lỗi, ghi lỗi vào sổ lỗi sai và đừng để AI viết lại bài giúp mình.

7  E2 IELTS (E2Language)PaidBand 5.5+ (from about US$76 for 90 days; free trial)

An online IELTS course with video lessons, live classes, mock tests and marked Writing and Speaking, from the team behind the E2 IELTS YouTube channel.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its higher packages give essays marked by expert tutors against the IELTS criteria within 48 hours, the personal feedback that self-study lacks.

How to use it: Use the free trial and the free E2 IELTS YouTube lessons first, and buy a package only when you need marked essays before your test.

Gợi ý: Học thử miễn phí và xem video YouTube của E2 trước; chỉ mua gói khi cần giáo viên chấm bài viết trước kỳ thi.

Checked on 27 October 2026. Free plans and prices can change.

chapters.html:
SPEAKING

The 7 best websites for speaking

Numbers 1–5 are free · 6 and 7 are paid options

Pick one or two websites and use them a little every day – that works better than trying them all once. Links open in a new tab.

1  Speak & Improve (Cambridge)Freeall levels (free, no account needed)

A free University of Cambridge research tool where you answer spoken questions and an AI 'speech robot' grades your speaking in seconds.

Why it helps for IELTS: It is a rare free way to speak aloud at home, get an instant CEFR grade (B2 ≈ Band 5.5–6.5, C1 ≈ Band 7–8) and try again to beat it.

How to use it: Do one practice test a week, listen back to your answers and re-record any answer graded below your target level.

Gợi ý: Mỗi tuần làm một bài luyện nói, nghe lại câu trả lời của mình và thu âm lại những câu bị chấm thấp.

2  IELTS Liz – SpeakingFree (paid extras)Band 5+ (free; optional paid lessons)

Free lessons on all three parts of the Speaking test, with current topic lists, model answers, tips and practice videos.

Why it helps for IELTS: Her Part 1–3 topics and model answers show students how long to speak and how to extend answers naturally.

How to use it: Pick one Part 2 topic a day, prepare for 1 minute, record yourself speaking for 2 minutes, then check it against her tips.

Gợi ý: Mỗi ngày chọn một đề Part 2, chuẩn bị 1 phút, tự ghi âm nói 2 phút rồi đối chiếu với các mẹo của Liz.

3  IDP IELTS – official Speaking samplesFreeall levels (free, no account needed)

Official recordings of an examiner and a candidate doing Speaking Parts 1, 2 and 3, with the questions and a full transcript.

Why it helps for IELTS: Hearing a real test from start to finish shows students the timing, question style and examiner language before test day.

How to use it: Pause after each examiner question and give your own answer aloud before you hear the candidate's.

Gợi ý: Nghe từng phần, dừng lại sau mỗi câu hỏi của giám khảo và tự trả lời thành tiếng trước khi nghe thí sinh trả lời.

4  BBC Learning English – PronunciationFreeall levels (free, no account needed)

Short BBC videos on English sounds, word stress, linking and intonation: Tim's Pronunciation Workshop and The Sounds of English.

Why it helps for IELTS: Pronunciation is a quarter of the Speaking score, and these videos train the sounds, stress and linking that make speech clear.

How to use it: Watch one Tim's Pronunciation Workshop episode a week and repeat every example aloud three times.

Website does not open on your internet? Use BBC Learning English on YouTube instead (same lessons).

Gợi ý: Mỗi tuần xem một tập Tim's Pronunciation Workshop và đọc to theo từng ví dụ ba lần.

5  YouGlishFreeall levels (free, no account needed)

A search tool that plays YouTube clips of real people saying any word or phrase, filtered by UK, US, Australian and other accents.

Why it helps for IELTS: Hearing a word in many real sentences fixes its stress and shows natural collocations to use in the Speaking test.

How to use it: Search each new word from this week's lesson, listen to 3–5 UK or Australian clips and repeat each sentence aloud.

Gợi ý: Tra từ mới của tuần, nghe 3–5 clip giọng Anh hoặc Úc rồi nhắc lại to từng câu.

Paid options – only if you want more

Very good, but they cost money. The free websites above are enough to reach your target band.

6  ELSA SpeakPaidall levels (small free version and 7-day trial; from 145,000₫ a month)

An AI pronunciation and speaking app, co-founded by Vietnamese entrepreneur Vu Van, that scores every word you say and shows which sounds to fix.

Why it helps for IELTS: Its instant sound-by-sound feedback helps students fix word stress and ending sounds, and Premium adds IELTS speaking practice.

How to use it: Use the 7-day trial for a 10-minute session every day, and subscribe only if you will keep practising daily.

Gợi ý: Dùng thử 7 ngày, luyện 10 phút mỗi ngày và chỉ mua gói trả phí nếu chắc chắn sẽ luyện đều đặn.

7  italki – IELTS tutorsPaidall levels (pay per lesson, about US$4–60 an hour; cheap trial lessons)

A marketplace of online one-to-one tutors where you can choose an IELTS-specialist teacher by price, accent and reviews.

Why it helps for IELTS: A real tutor can run full mock Speaking tests and give band-based feedback, which no app fully replaces.

How to use it: Book two or three cheap trial lessons with different IELTS tutors, then do one mock Speaking test a week with the best one.

Gợi ý: Đặt vài buổi học thử giá rẻ với các giáo viên IELTS khác nhau, rồi chọn một người để thi thử Speaking mỗi tuần.

WEEK 1

Listening + Speaking

Listening Part 1 · Speaking Part 1

This week you will
  • understand how IELTS is scored and what Band 6, 7 and 8 mean
  • catch names, numbers and spelling in Listening Part 1 — and avoid the distractors
  • give natural, extended answers in Speaking Part 1 using A–R–E
Practice audio
  • Warm-up dictation (letters and numbers)
  • Mini Part 1 practice (hotel booking)
  • Speaking Part 1 practice with the examiner
Common mistakes Vietnamese learners make

Listening

  • Missing plural -s (ticket → tickets, book → books)
  • Misspelling familiar words (February, Thursday, restaurant, necessary)
  • Mixing up numbers: 13/30, 14/40, 15/50
  • Mixing up letters: A/E/I, G/J, B/V, and saying H as “hát”
  • Writing the first answer you hear (distractors!) and too many words

Speaking

  • One-word answers, or long memorised speeches
  • I am live… → I live…; I very like… → I really like…
  • Missing verb to be: My hometown very beautiful
  • Dropping ending sounds: book instead of books, like instead of liked

Which level should I choose? (Chọn mức độ nào?)

  • Easy (Band 5–5.5) — English is still hard for you, or you are new to IELTS.
  • Medium (Band 6–6.5) — your level is around Band 5.5–6.
  • Challenging (Band 7–7.5) — you are aiming for Band 7 or higher.
  • Want more practice? Do your level first, then try the next one.
Your daily 15-minute listening habit
  1. Listen once to a short clip (3–5 minutes) without the script. What is it about?
  2. Listen again with the transcript. Highlight the “dark areas” — the words you could not hear. Say them aloud.
  3. Shadow 3–5 sentences: play, pause, repeat with the same speed and rhythm.

Free sources: BBC Learning English (try 6 Minute English) · British Council LearnEnglish – Listening · TED-Ed

Bonus (optional): real exam practice

Cambridge IELTS 17 · Test 1 · Listening Part 1 — materials not included; use your own copy of the book.

WEEK 1

Answers & Transcripts

Answers and explanations for all homework quizzes

How to use this page

  • Listening: play the recording and read the transcript at the same time. Stop at every highlighted answer and ask: What did I hear? What did I write? Why was it different? The parts you could not hear are your “dark areas” — shadow them 3 times.
  • Reading: read each paragraph again, then its summary in simple English and in Vietnamese.
  • Writing and Speaking: read the explanations, then read the sample answers aloud.

Jump to: Listening · Reading · Writing · Speaking

Listening

W1 Listening · Easy (Band 5–5.5)

Listening · Easy — Hiring bikes

Practice test, week one. Listening, Part 1. Easy level.

You will hear a woman called Anna phoning a shop to hire some bikes. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.

Shop assistant (Tom): Hello, Riverside Bike Hire. This is Tom speaking. How can I help you?

Anna: Hello. I'd like to hire some bikes for this weekend, please.

Shop assistant (Tom): Of course. Can I have your name, please?

Anna: Yes. My name is Anna Parker.

Shop assistant (Tom): How do you spell your surname?

Anna: It's P, A, R, K, E, R.

Shop assistant (Tom): Thank you, Ms Parker. How many bikes do you need?

Anna: We're a family of five, but my daughter is only two, so she can sit in a child seat on my bike. So we need four bikes.

Shop assistant (Tom): Four bikes. That's fine. The child seat is free. And which day would you like them?

Anna: Not Saturday, because my son has a football match. Can we have them on Sunday?

Shop assistant (Tom): Yes, Sunday is fine. What time would you like to collect the bikes?

Anna: What time do you open?

Why We Forget — and How to Remember More

A  Most language learners know the feeling. On Monday you learn twenty new words, and by Friday you can only remember five or six. It is easy to believe that this happens because you are not clever enough, or because English is simply too difficult. In fact, forgetting is a completely normal part of how the human brain works — and understanding it can help you study more effectively.

In simple English: Forgetting new words quickly is normal — it is how the brain works. Understanding it helps you study better.

B  One of the first people to study forgetting scientifically was the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus. In the 1880s, he spent several years testing his own memory. To make sure that his existing knowledge did not help him, he invented thousands of meaningless syllables, such as ‘WID’ and ‘ZOF’, and learned lists of them by heart. He then measured how much he could still remember after different periods of time. His results, published in 1885, showed that forgetting happens fastest at the very beginning. Within an hour, more than half of a new list had gone, and after one day only around a third remained. After that, the speed of forgetting slowed down considerably. When these results are drawn on a graph, they form a shape that is now known as the ‘forgetting curve’.

In simple English: In the 1880s, Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with meaningless syllables. He found that we forget fastest at the beginning: the ‘forgetting curve’.

C  Ebbinghaus also discovered something more encouraging: each time he reviewed a list, he forgot it more slowly afterwards. In other words, every review makes a memory stronger and longer-lasting. He also found that reviews spread out over several days were far more effective than the same number of reviews done all at once. Today, this is called the ‘spacing effect’, and it is one of the most reliable findings in the whole of psychology.

In simple English: Every review makes a memory stronger. Reviews spread over several days work best: the ‘spacing effect’.

Tiếng Việt: Mỗi lần ôn lại, ta quên chậm hơn. Ôn rải rác trong nhiều ngày hiệu quả hơn ôn dồn một lúc — gọi là “hiệu ứng giãn cách”.

For a language, which has to be used for years rather than for one exam, this is a very poor strategy.

In simple English: Cramming the night before an exam may help the next morning, but the information is soon forgotten.

Tiếng Việt: Học nhồi nhét đêm trước kỳ thi có thể giúp qua bài kiểm tra sáng hôm sau, nhưng sẽ quên rất nhanh — cách này không phù hợp để học ngoại ngữ.

The Hidden Difficulty of Listening

A  Ask language learners which skill they find hardest, and many will name listening. This can seem surprising, since listening is often described as a ‘passive’ skill, in contrast to the ‘active’ skills of speaking and writing. Yet researchers now agree that this description is misleading. Understanding speech is one of the most demanding tasks the brain performs, and doing it in a second language adds several layers of difficulty that readers never face.

In simple English: Listening is often called a ‘passive’ skill, but it is really one of the hardest jobs for the brain — especially in a second language.

Tiếng Việt: Nghe thường bị coi là kỹ năng “thụ động”, nhưng thật ra đây là một việc rất khó với não bộ, nhất là khi nghe ngoại ngữ.

B  The first problem is that speech, unlike writing, does not contain clear gaps between words. On a printed page, every word is separated by a space; in natural conversation, words run into one another, sounds disappear and neighbouring sounds change each other. A phrase such as ‘want to go’ may be pronounced as something closer to ‘wanna go’, while ‘next day’ typically loses its final ‘t’. Native listeners divide this continuous stream into words without noticing that they are doing so. Second-language listeners, however, must often work this out consciously, and they tend to rely on the habits of their first language, which may not suit the new one. The psycholinguist Anne Cutler, whose research on this subject is summarised in her book Native Listening, has shown that listeners from different language backgrounds use quite different cues to find word boundaries.

In simple English: In speech, words run together and sounds change, so learners must work out where each word starts and ends.

Tiếng Việt: Khi nói, các từ dính liền nhau và âm bị nuốt hoặc biến đổi (ví dụ “want to go” → “wanna go”). Người học phải tự tách từ, và thường áp dụng thói quen của tiếng mẹ đẻ.

C  A second difficulty concerns time. A reader controls the speed of the text: it is possible to slow down, reread a difficult sentence or look back at an earlier paragraph. A listener has none of these options. Speech arrives at the speaker’s pace, often around 150 to 200 words per minute in conversation, and each word must be processed before the next one arrives. If a listener stops to think about an unfamiliar word, the following sentence may be lost entirely.

In simple English: Readers can slow down or read again, but listeners cannot: speech comes at 150–200 words a minute.

Tiếng Việt: Người đọc có thể đọc chậm hay đọc lại, còn người nghe thì không: người nói nói khoảng 150–200 từ mỗi phút, dừng lại nghĩ về một từ là mất câu tiếp theo.

D  This points to the role of working memory, the limited mental space in which we hold and manipulate information for short periods. When listening in a first language, recognising words is largely automatic, which leaves working memory free for understanding ideas, making predictions and connecting new information to what was said earlier. For less proficient second-language listeners, word recognition itself consumes much of this capacity. As a result, there is little left over for interpreting meaning, and comprehension breaks down even when the vocabulary is, in principle, known.

In simple English: Working memory is small. Weaker listeners use most of it just to recognise words, so little is left for understanding.

Tiếng Việt: Trí nhớ làm việc có dung lượng nhỏ. Người nghe trình độ thấp phải dùng gần hết để nhận ra từng từ, nên không còn đủ “chỗ” để hiểu ý.

E  Pronunciation differences between languages create further obstacles. Vietnamese, for instance, has no consonant clusters, and its words end in only a small set of consonants, which are usually not fully released. English, by contrast, frequently places two or three consonants together at the end of words — as in ‘texts’ or ‘asked’ — and uses these final sounds to carry important grammatical information, such as plural forms and the past tense. Learners whose first language does not mark these endings may simply fail to hear them, which helps to explain why answers such as ‘book’ instead of ‘books’ are among the most common errors in listening tests.

In simple English: Vietnamese has no consonant clusters and few final sounds, so Vietnamese learners often do not hear English endings such as plural -s.

F  Fortunately, the research also suggests ways forward. Because word recognition becomes faster with practice, extensive listening to material that is only slightly above a learner’s current level appears to build the automatic processing that skilled listening depends on. Specific techniques can also help. Dictation trains attention to small words and word endings; ‘shadowing’, in which learners repeat a recording aloud almost simultaneously, links listening to pronunciation; and transcription work — comparing what one thought one heard with the actual script — reveals the sound patterns that are being misheard. Over time, these activities allow learners to shift from decoding individual words to following ideas, which is, after all, the real purpose of listening.

In simple English: Practice helps: listen a lot to slightly difficult material, and use dictation, shadowing and transcription.

4Living abroad is very expensive.

Every sentence needs a verb (is). Use the -ing form as the subject: Living abroad is …

5She wants to be a teacher.

Use a / an before a job: a teacher, an engineer.

6People in many countries learn English.

many + plural noun: many countries (country → countries). much is for uncountable nouns (much time).

7I want to improve my English.

want to + verb: I want to improve, I want to live abroad.

8It is cheap because you can study at home.

A sentence that starts with Because is not complete on its own. Join the two ideas: It is cheap because you can study at home.

Part B · the complete Band 5 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

Nowadays, many people want to learn a foreign language. Some people think that (9) living in another country is the best way to learn it. I (10) agree with this idea for two reasons.

First, when you live in a foreign country, you (11) have to use the language every day. For (12) example, you need to speak English when you buy food, take a bus or talk to your (13) neighbours. (14) Because of this, you can practise a lot and learn new words (15) quickly. (16) Also, your listening will improve because you hear native speakers all the time.

Second, living abroad helps you to understand the culture of the country. Language and culture are connected. If you know the culture, you can understand jokes and films more easily. My cousin (17) lived in Australia for two years, and now he speaks English very well.

(18) However, living in another country is very expensive, so not everyone can do it. People can also learn a language at home if they (19) study hard, for example, with online lessons and English films.

In (20) conclusion, I agree that living in a country where the language is spoken is the best way to learn it, because you use the language every day and you learn about the culture. But people who cannot go abroad can still learn at home.

Why this is a Band 5 answer

  • ✔ A clear opinion in the introduction (I agree) and again in the conclusion.
  • ✔ Two simple reasons, each with a short explanation and an example.
  • ✔ Basic linking words: First, Second, For example, Also, However, In conclusion.
  • ✔ Mostly simple sentences with correct grammar (he speaks, my cousin lived, if they study).
  • ✘ Ideas are not developed much, and vocabulary is basic and repeated (learn, language, country).
  • To reach Band 6: explain each reason in more detail and use some longer sentences (with which, although, so) — compare the Band 6 sample.
W1 Writing · Medium (Band 6–6.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1Nowadays, the internet plays an important role in our lives.

There is only one internet → the internet. Role is countable → an important role. Our = many people → lives.

2We can find a lot of information on the internet.

Information is uncountable: no -s, use a lot of / much. We say on the internet.

3Learning English helps students find better jobs.

An -ing subject (Learning English) is singular → helps. Pattern: help + someone + (to) do.

4Since 2020, the number of online learners has increased rapidly.

Since + a point in time → present perfect. The number of → singular verb (has).

5E-books are cheap, and they are also easy to buy.

Two full sentences cannot be joined with only a comma (comma splice). Use and, a full stop or a semicolon.

6convenient

convenient (adjective after very) · impact on · In my opinion, (In my opinion, I think says the same thing twice; According to me is not natural English).

7on(see above)
8In my opinion,(see above)

Part B · the complete Band 6 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

These days, more and more people are learning foreign languages, and some believe that living in a country where the language is spoken is the most (9) effective way to learn it. In my opinion, this is true to a large (10) extent, although it is not the only way.

The main (11) advantage of living abroad is that learners are (12) surrounded by the language all day. They have to communicate in it when they go shopping, use public transport or deal with problems at work. As a (13) result, they practise far more than students in a classroom, and they quickly learn useful everyday (14) expressions. In (15) addition, they get used to the natural speed and different (16) accents of native speakers, which is difficult to learn from textbooks.

On the other (17) hand, living in another country does not automatically make someone fluent. For example, a friend of mine spent three years in Canada, but he mainly spent time with other Vietnamese people, so his English did not (18) improve much. This shows that being surrounded by a language is not enough without effort. (19) Furthermore, many people cannot afford to live overseas, so they need other options, such as online classes, films with subtitles and conversation practice with native speakers on the internet.

In (20) conclusion, I agree that living in a country where a language is spoken is usually the best way to learn it, because learners use the language constantly. However, success depends on how actively people practise, and those who stay at home can also reach a high level if they study regularly.

Why this is a Band 6 answer

  • ✔ A clear position (true to a large extent, but not the only way) that stays the same until the conclusion.
  • ✔ Each body paragraph has one main idea, with reasons and a personal example.
  • ✔ A range of linking phrases: As a result, In addition, On the other hand, Furthermore.
  • ✔ A mix of simple and complex sentences (which…, so…, although…) with few errors.
  • ✘ Vocabulary is good but fairly common; some ideas could be explained more precisely.
  • To reach Band 7: use more precise, less common vocabulary and develop each idea further — compare the Band 7 sample.
W1 Writing · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1The number of people who learn English online has risen sharply.

The number of → singular verb (has); people who learn (people = plural).

2Despite the high cost, many families invest in English classes.

Despite + noun (no of). Before a clause, use Although the cost is high.

3Although technology is useful, it can also be distracting.

Vietnamese says “mặc dù … nhưng …”, but English uses only one linker: Although X, Y.

4Scientists have done a lot of research on this problem.

Research is uncountable, and the collocation is do / carry out / conduct research (not make).

5This essay will discuss both views.

discuss something (no about) — but a discussion about something.

6Some people believe that all pupils ought to be required to study a second language.

The best paraphrase changes words and structure but keeps the meaning. A copies the original; C changes the meaning (important ≠ compulsory).

7Children nowadays spend an excessive amount of time on their phones.

Task 2 needs a neutral, academic tone: avoid slang (kids, glued, 24/7) and spoken fillers (you know).

8Every student needs to practise speaking regularly.

Every + singular noun + singular verb: every student needs.

Part B · the complete Band 7 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

It is often (9) argued that the most effective way to master a foreign language is to live in a country where it is spoken. While I accept that (10) immersion offers unique advantages, I believe it is only the best option for learners who are willing to (11) engage actively with the local community.

(12) Admittedly, living abroad provides an (13) intensity of exposure that no classroom can match. Learners are constantly (14) required to understand and respond in real situations, from negotiating a rental contract to making small talk with colleagues. This not only (15) accelerates the development of listening and speaking skills, but also helps learners (16) acquire the idiomatic expressions and cultural knowledge that textbooks rarely cover. (17) Moreover, the need to communicate in order to get through daily life is a powerful motivator.

(18) However, immersion alone does not guarantee success. Many expatriates live overseas for years yet remain at a basic level, either because they socialise mainly with people from their own country (19) or because they lack a solid grasp of grammar. Without systematic study, they tend to rely on a limited set of phrases and repeat the same errors. (20) Conversely, highly motivated learners who never leave their home country can achieve impressive fluency by combining structured lessons with regular online conversation practice and extensive exposure to authentic material such as podcasts and films.

In conclusion, although living in a country where a language is spoken can be extremely beneficial, it is not inherently the best method. The decisive factor is how actively learners use the opportunities available to them, wherever they happen to live.

Why this is a Band 7 answer

  • ✔ A clear, nuanced position: immersion helps, but only for learners who use it actively.
  • ✔ Both sides are developed with specific examples (a rental contract, small talk, expatriates who stay at a basic level).
  • ✔ Less common vocabulary used precisely: immersion, intensity of exposure, expatriates, systematic study, authentic material.
  • ✔ Complex structures: not only … but also, either … or, While I accept that …
  • To reach Band 8: keep this range but make every idea fully extended and the word choice even more precise, with no slips.

Speaking

W1 Speaking · Easy (Band 5–5.5)
QAnswerWhy
1books

After p, t, k, f the -s sounds like /s/: books, cats. After other sounds it is /z/: dogs, pens.

2fifty

FIFty, but fifTEEN, sixTEEN. Numbers ending in -ty are stressed at the start.

3I’m a student.

Use a / an before a job or role: I’m a student, I’m an engineer.

4Yes, I do. I work in a bank, and my colleagues are very friendly.

Answer, then add one or two details. Yes, I like is wrong: say Yes, I do or Yes, I like it.

5I like music very much.

very much goes at the end: I like music very much. You can also say I really like music.

6know

know /nəʊ/: the k is silent, so know and no sound the same.

7About twice a week, usually at the weekend.

How often needs a frequency: every day, twice a week, once a month.

8My hometown has many beautiful places.

My hometown = it → has. Never put is before have.

9watched

After p, k, s, sh, ch the -ed sounds like /t/: watched /wɒtʃt/. played = /d/, wanted = /ɪd/.

10The city, because there are more jobs and things to do.

Choose one, then give a reason with because.

11Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?

In Part 1 you can ask the examiner to repeat the question. It is polite and you do not lose marks.

12Yesterday I went to the market.

Yesterday = past → went (go – went – gone).

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Where is your hometown?
My hometown is Hai Phong. It’s a big city in the north of Vietnam, near the sea.

Do you work or are you a student?
I’m a student. I study accounting at a university in Hanoi.

What do you do in your free time?
I usually watch films or play football with my friends. It helps me relax after school.

Do you like your hometown?
Yes, I do. The people are very friendly, and the seafood is really good.

W1 Speaking · Medium (Band 6–6.5)
QAnswerWhy
1watches

After s, z, sh, ch, j sounds, -s/-es = /ɪz/: watch·es, bus·es, page·s.

2bags

After a voiced sound (g, b, d, v, vowels) -s = /z/: bags, dogs, plays. After p, t, k, f it is /s/: cats, maps.

3thirteen

thirTEEN vs THIRty. The long “teen” and the stress help listeners (and you!) tell 13 from 30.

4Yes, I really do. It's a small coastal town, so life there is quite relaxed, and the seafood is amazing.

Answer + reason + extra detail. The second answer has two common errors: I like (needs an object or I do) and a missing verb (is very beautiful).

5I live in Da Nang.

Never am + verb. Use I live (fact) or I'm living (temporary).

6I'm really into football.

Very cannot go before like. Natural options: I'm really into…, I really like…, I like … very much.

7I've lived there since 2015.

Since / for + an action that continues now → present perfect: I've lived there since 2015.

8I prefer coffee because it keeps me awake when I study late at night.

Give a direct answer, then a reason (because…).

9listen

listen /ˈlɪsn/: the t is silent. More silent letters: know (k), half (l), Wednesday (d).

10music

MUsic, but hoTEL and poLICE.

11I'm bored at weekends.

bored = how you feel; boring = the thing that makes you feel bored (The film was boring, so I was bored).

12Mostly pop, especially Vietnamese ballads, because they help me relax after a long day.

A direct answer, a detail and a reason: A–R–E.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Where is your hometown?
I’m from Hue, in central Vietnam. It’s a fairly small city on the Perfume River, and it used to be the capital a long time ago.

What do you like most about it?
Probably how peaceful it is. Life moves much more slowly than in Ho Chi Minh City, and in the evening you can just sit by the river and relax.

What do you usually do in your free time?
I usually go jogging in the park near my house, and at the weekend I like watching movies with my friends — mostly comedies.

Have your hobbies changed since you were a child?
Yes, quite a lot. When I was a child, I used to play football every afternoon. These days I don’t have much time, so I prefer jogging. In the future I’d like to try something new, like rock climbing.

W1 Speaking · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)
QAnswerWhy
1photography

PHOtograph · phoTOgraphy · photoGRAPHic. Wrong stress makes words hard to recognise.

2wanted

Only after t or d: want·ed, need·ed. asked = /ɑːskt/ (one syllable), played = /pleɪd/.

3Yes, I'm quite keen on it, actually, especially at weekends, when I've got time to try out new recipes.

B paraphrases (keen on) and adds a detail. A repeats cooking three times; C sounds memorised and far too formal for Part 1.

4I'd say evenings, to be honest.

An either/or question needs a choice, not Yes, I do. Avoid essay-style openings in Part 1.

5I stay up late and feel more active at night.

A night owl stays up late; an early bird gets up early. Natural idioms like these help Lexical Resource.

6When I was a child, I used to collect stamps.

used to + verb = a past habit. be used to + -ing means “be familiar with”.

7I've been working here for three years.

for + a length of time; since + a point in time (since 2023).

8I think so, yes. Back when I was growing up, everyone on our street knew each other, whereas these days people tend to keep to themselves, partly because we're all so busy.

Past vs present contrast (whereas), correct tenses and a reason (partly because…).

9That's an interesting question — let me think for a second.

Short thinking phrases keep you fluent: That's an interesting question…, Let me see…, Well, …

10“wanna” /ˈwɒnə/

want to → wanna, going to → gonna. You don’t have to say them, but you must recognise them when you listen.

11Not as much as I used to, to be honest. These days I mostly read on my phone, but I still love a good crime novel on holiday.

A natural opener, past vs present (used to) and a specific detail. The last answer sounds memorised.

12I can't get enough of it.

I can't get enough of it = I love it. Not a big fan = I don't like it much; take it or leave it = I don't mind either way.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

What do you find most challenging about your work or studies?
Honestly, it’s juggling everything. I work full-time, so finding the energy to study in the evenings is a real struggle — some nights I just can’t focus.

Has the kind of music you like changed over the years?
Definitely. As a teenager I was really into K-pop, but these days I tend to listen to acoustic stuff and podcasts — I suppose my taste has mellowed as I’ve got older.

Do you think people were closer to their neighbours in the past?
I’d say so, yes. Back when I was growing up, everyone on our street knew each other and kids would wander in and out of each other’s houses. Nowadays, especially in apartment blocks, people tend to keep themselves to themselves, partly because everyone’s so busy.

chapters.html:
WEEK 2

Reading + Writing

Skimming, scanning and True / False / Not Given · Writing Task 1: line graphs

This week you will
  • skim a passage for the main ideas and scan it for names, numbers and key words
  • tell TRUE, FALSE and NOT GIVEN apart — the question type many Vietnamese students find hardest
  • write a Writing Task 1 report on a line graph: introduction, overview and trends
Practice audio
  • Warm-up: numbers in context
Common mistakes Vietnamese learners make

Reading

  • Reading every word and translating it into Vietnamese → no time left
  • Choosing FALSE when the passage simply does not say (that is NOT GIVEN)
  • Using your own knowledge instead of the passage
  • Missing the small words: all, most, only, never, first
  • Breaking the word limit (ONE WORD ONLY)

Writing

  • No overview — or an overview full of numbers
  • The price raised → The price rose; increase → increased (past years)
  • The amount of people → The number of people; 40% students → 40% of students
  • Listing every number instead of choosing the main features
  • Giving opinions or reasons (“because people love their phones”)
Homework — choose your level for each skill
SkillEasy
Band 5–5.5		Medium
Band 6–6.5		Challenging

ListeningEasyMediumChallenging10–15 min
ReadingEasyMediumChallenging15–20 min

Which level should I choose? (Chọn mức độ nào?)

  • Easy (Band 5–5.5) — English is still hard for you, or you are new to IELTS.
  • Medium (Band 6–6.5) — your level is around Band 5.5–6.
  • Challenging (Band 7–7.5) — you are aiming for Band 7 or higher.
  • Want more practice? Do your level first, then try the next one.
Your daily 15-minute listening habit
  1. Listen once to a short clip (3–5 minutes) without the script. What is it about?
  2. Listen again with the transcript. Highlight the “dark areas” — the words you could not hear. Say them aloud.
  3. Shadow 3–5 sentences: play, pause, repeat with the same speed and rhythm.

Free sources: BBC Learning English (try 6 Minute English) · British Council LearnEnglish – Listening · TED-Ed

Bonus (optional): real exam practice

Cambridge IELTS 17 · Test 4 · Reading Passage 1 (True / False / Not Given) and Writing Task 1 (line graph) — materials not included; use your own copy of the book.

Answers & Transcripts

Answers and explanations for all homework quizzes

How to use this page

  • Listening: play the recording and read the transcript at the same time. Stop at every highlighted answer and ask: What did I hear? What did I write? Why was it different? The parts you could not hear are your “dark areas” — shadow them 3 times.

  • Writing and Speaking: read the explanations, then read the sample answers aloud.

Jump to: Listening · Reading · Writing · Speaking

Listening

Listening · Easy — Coach trips

Practice test, week two. Listening, Part 1. Easy level.

You will hear a man called David phoning a tourist information centre to ask about coach trips. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.

Tourist office (Lucy): Good morning, Kingsford Tourist Information. Lucy speaking. How can I help you?

David: Hello. My parents are coming to visit me next week, and I'd like to take them on a day trip. Do you have any coach trips?

Tourist office (Lucy): Yes, we do. Next week there are three trips. The first one goes to Hadley Castle and its gardens. That's on Tuesday.

David: A castle. My father would like that. What time does the coach leave?

Tourist office (Lucy): It leaves the bus station at nine o'clock in the morning.

David: And how much does it cost?

Tourist office (Lucy): Last year it was sixteen pounds, but this year the price for adults is eighteen pounds.

David: Eighteen pounds. OK. What does the price include?

Tourist office (Lucy): It includes a guided tour of the castle. A guide takes you round and tells you about its history. Lunch isn't included, but there's a nice café in the gardens.

David: And what's the second trip?

Tourist office (Lucy): That's the lake and boat trip. It was on Wednesday last year, but this year it's on Thursday. The coach leaves at half past eight, and the price is twenty-five pounds.

David: Twenty-five pounds. Is lunch included in that?

Tourist office (Lucy): Yes, it is. You have lunch on the boat. But it can be cold and windy on the lake. An umbrella isn't much use in the wind, so please bring a warm jacket.

David: A warm jacket. Good idea. And the third trip?

Tourist office (Lucy): The third trip goes to Port Ellen. It's a pretty little town by the sea. That's on Saturday. The coach leaves at ten o'clock. Oh, sorry, no. That's last month's timetable. It leaves at quarter past ten.

David: Quarter past ten. And the price?

Tourist office (Lucy): Fifteen pounds. There's a lot to see in Port Ellen. The aquarium costs eight pounds to go in, but the museum is free, and it's very interesting.

Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.

David: My father loves history, so I think the castle trip is the best one for us.

Tourist office (Lucy): It's very popular. But there's a lot of walking in the gardens. About three kilometres.

David: Oh. My mother has a bad knee, so she can't walk very far. Then the lake and boat trip is better. They can sit on the boat and enjoy the view.

Tourist office (Lucy): Good choice. So that's three tickets for the boat trip on Thursday.

David: Can I pay by card now, on the phone?

Tourist office (Lucy): I'm sorry, our card machine isn't working today. You can come to the office and pay in cash, or you can pay online on our website.

David: I'm not in town this week, so I'll pay online tonight.

Tourist office (Lucy): That's fine. Now, the coach for the boat trip doesn't leave from the bus station. It leaves from outside the town hall, in Market Square.

David: The town hall. OK. Should we arrive early?

Tourist office (Lucy): There's no need to arrive early. Just be there on time. But please book soon. There are only a few seats left, and the trips are very popular in summer.

David: I'll do it tonight, then. Thank you very much for your help.

Tourist office (Lucy): You're welcome. Enjoy your trip!

That is the end of Part 1.

Listening · Medium — Renting a flat

Practice test, week two. Listening, Part 1. Medium level.

You will hear a student called Liam phoning a letting agency about flats to rent. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.

Letting agent (Rachel): Good afternoon, City Lettings. Rachel speaking.

Liam: Oh, hi. I'm a student at the university, and I'm looking for a one-bedroom flat from September. I saw on your website that you've got a few available.

Letting agent (Rachel): That's right. We've got three at the moment that might suit you. Can I ask what your budget is?

Liam: Ideally no more than seven hundred pounds a month.

Letting agent (Rachel): OK. The first one is on Danbury Street. That's D, A, N, B, U, R, Y.

Liam: Danbury Street. And which number?

Letting agent (Rachel): Fourteen. The rent is six hundred and fifty pounds a month. The best thing about it is the location. People often say it's near the park, but actually the park is a fifteen-minute walk away. What it is close to is the station. It's only two minutes' walk, so getting to the campus is easy.

Liam: Sounds good. Any problems with it?

Letting agent (Rachel): Well, it's quite an old building, but the bathroom was redone last year, so that's fine. The main drawback is the kitchen. It's tiny. There's hardly room for two people.

Liam: Right. And the second one?

Letting agent (Rachel): That's number nine, Park Road. It's a lovely flat on the fourth floor, with a big balcony, and it's very quiet. The advert says six hundred and twenty pounds, but the landlord has just reduced the rent to five hundred and ninety-five.

Liam: Five hundred and ninety-five. That's well within my budget. What's the catch?

Letting agent (Rachel): The heating is brand new, so that's not a problem. The downside is that there's no lift, so you'd have to carry your shopping up four floors.

Liam: Hmm. I suppose that would keep me fit. And the third flat?

Letting agent (Rachel): That's twenty-seven Hill Avenue. It's in a modern building, and the rent is a bit higher, at seven hundred and twenty pounds. The furniture isn't included, I'm afraid, but all the bills are: gas, electricity and the internet.

Liam: That does make a difference. Is it far from the university?

Letting agent (Rachel): It's about twenty-five minutes by bus.

Can We Really Learn to Read Faster?

A  Every year, millions of people sign up for courses or download apps that promise to double or even triple their reading speed. The idea is attractive: if we could read three times faster, we could get through three times as many books, reports and emails. But can reading really be speeded up so easily? Instead, they make a series of rapid jumps, called saccades, and between these jumps they stop briefly on a word. When Graphs Mislead

A  Charts and graphs are often seen as the most objective way of presenting information. A table of numbers can be difficult to interpret, but a line that climbs steeply or a bar that towers over its neighbours appears to speak for itself. It is precisely this impression of clarity that makes visual data so persuasive — and, in the wrong hands, so open to misuse. A graph does not need to contain a single false number in order to give a false impression.

In simple English: Graphs look objective and clear, which makes them persuasive — and easy to misuse, even without any false numbers.

Tiếng Việt: Biểu đồ trông khách quan và rõ ràng nên rất thuyết phục — nhưng cũng dễ bị lợi dụng: không cần số liệu sai vẫn có thể tạo ra ấn tượng sai.

B  Concern about misleading visuals is far from new. In 1954, the American writer Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a short and humorous book that became one of the best-selling statistics books ever written. Huff devoted a chapter to what he called the ‘gee-whiz graph’, in which a modest change is made to look dramatic. Almost three decades later, the statistician and designer Edward Tufte proposed a way of measuring such distortion. His ‘lie factor’, introduced in The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983), compares the size of an effect as it is shown in a graphic with the size of the effect in the data itself. In an honest graphic, the two are equal and the lie factor is one.

In simple English: The problem is old: Darrell Huff wrote about the ‘gee-whiz graph’ in 1954, and Edward Tufte’s ‘lie factor’ (1983) measures how much a graphic exaggerates the data.

Tiếng Việt: Vấn đề này không mới: năm 1954 Darrell Huff đã viết về biểu đồ “gee-whiz” (làm thay đổi nhỏ trông như rất lớn); năm 1983 Edward Tufte đưa ra “hệ số nói dối” (lie factor) — biểu đồ trung thực có hệ số bằng 1.

C  The most common technique is to truncate the vertical axis, so that it starts not at zero but just below the smallest value. Suppose that a company’s sales rise from 50 to 52 million dollars. On a scale from zero to 60, the increase is barely visible; on a scale from 49 to 53, the same 4 per cent rise appears as a line that shoots upwards, exaggerating a modest change. Similar effects can be created by stretching or squeezing one axis, by choosing a starting year that flatters the trend, or by plotting two different measures against two separate vertical axes, which can make almost any pair of variables appear to move together. Three-dimensional pie charts are another frequent offender: tilting the circle makes the slices at the front look larger than equally sized slices at the back.

In simple English: The most common trick is a vertical axis that does not start at zero; stretched axes, carefully chosen start dates, two separate axes and 3D pie charts can also mislead.

Tiếng Việt: Thủ thuật phổ biến nhất là trục tung không bắt đầu từ 0 (mức tăng 4% trông như tăng vọt). Kéo giãn trục, chọn năm bắt đầu có lợi, dùng hai trục tung hoặc biểu đồ tròn 3D cũng gây hiểu lầm.

D  Experimental research confirms that such choices affect readers. In a study presented in 2015, a team at New York University showed participants charts that had been distorted with common techniques, including truncated axes, and found that many viewers interpreted the message in its exaggerated form. A later study by Michael Correll and his colleagues, published in 2020, produced an even more troubling result: the impression created by a truncated axis persisted even when the chart carried a clear visual signal that the axis had been cut. In other words, knowing that a graph has been manipulated does not necessarily protect us from its influence.

In simple English: Studies from 2015 and 2020 show that distorted charts really do mislead people — even when they are warned that the axis has been cut.

Tiếng Việt: Các nghiên cứu năm 2015 và 2020 cho thấy biểu đồ bị bóp méo thật sự đánh lừa người xem — kể cả khi biểu đồ có dấu hiệu cho biết trục đã bị cắt.

E  It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that every truncated axis is dishonest. Correll’s team pointed out that whether truncation is appropriate depends on what the chart is intended to communicate. For a bar chart, where readers judge quantities by the length of the bars, starting at zero is generally essential. For a line graph showing, for example, a patient’s body temperature, a scale beginning at zero would hide differences of a degree or two that are medically important. The key question is not whether the axis starts at zero but whether the scale matches the size of the differences that matter.

In simple English: Not every cut axis is dishonest: bar charts should start at zero, but a line graph of body temperature needs a narrow scale. The scale should match the differences that matter.

Tiếng Việt: Không phải cứ cắt trục là gian dối: biểu đồ cột nên bắt đầu từ 0, nhưng biểu đồ đường về nhiệt độ cơ thể cần thang đo hẹp. Điều quan trọng là thang đo phù hợp với mức chênh lệch có ý nghĩa.

F  For readers, the most effective defence is a habit of active scepticism. Before reacting to the shape of a line, it is worth checking the labels and units on both axes, noting where the scale begins and asking what period of time has been selected — and what might have happened just outside it. It also helps to remember that every one of these features was chosen by the person who designed the chart, and to ask why. For candidates in the IELTS Writing test, the lesson works in reverse. Task 1 asks them to report the main features of a chart accurately, which means describing changes in proportion to their real size: a rise from 50 to 52 is ‘slight’, however steep the line may appear.

In simple English: Readers should check the labels, units, where the scale starts and the time period. In IELTS Task 1, describe changes by their real size: 50 to 52 is a slight rise.

Part B · the complete Band 5 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

The line graph shows the number of hours that young people aged 16 to 24 in one country spent on three activities every week (9) from 2005 to 2025. The activities are watching TV, using social media and reading.

(10) Overall, the time spent on social media (11) increased a lot, but the time spent watching TV went (12) down. Reading did not change very much.

In 2005, young people watched TV for 16 hours a week. After that, this number (13) fell, and in 2025 it was only 7 hours. On the other (14) hand, social media was not popular in 2005. Young people used it for only 2 hours a week. Then the number went up (15) quickly to 11 hours in 2015 and 18 hours in 2025. In 2025, young people spent more time on social media (16) than on TV.

Young people read for 6 hours a week in 2005. This went down (17) to 4 hours in 2015, and after that it stayed the (18) same. From 2010, reading was (19) the least popular activity. In 2025, young people spent (20) much more time on social media than on reading.

Why this is a Band 5 answer

  • ✔ It has an overview (Overall, …) with the main changes.
  • ✔ The key numbers for each activity are correct.
  • ✔ The past simple is used correctly (watched, fell, went down, stayed).
  • ✘ The numbers are mostly listed one year after another, with few comparisons. The overview does not say that social media overtook TV.
  • ✘ The vocabulary is basic and repeated (went up, went down, a lot).
  • To reach Band 6: use a range of trend words (rose steadily, fell gradually, remained stable) and compare the lines — look at the Band 6 sample.
W2 Writing · Medium (Band 6–6.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1Sales rose by 20,000.

by = the size of the change (+20,000); to = the final number (70,000). So: Sales rose by 20,000, to 70,000.

2The percentage of students who cycled to school rose.

the percentage of + a plural noun (students), and rose: rise – rose – risen has no object, while raise needs one (raise prices). Use percent after a number: 40 percent.

3There was a decrease of 10% in the number of visitors.

a decrease of + the size (10%) · a decrease in + the thing that changed (the number of visitors).

4The number of visitors peaked at 2 million in 2015.

peak at + the number · in + the year. (Also: reach a peak of 2 million.)

5The number of electric cars is expected to rise to 5 million by 2030.

Future years are predictions: is expected / predicted / projected to + verb, or will + verb.

6rose steadily

rose steadily (verb + adverb) · while joins two different trends (despite / because of + noun) · By 2020, … had overtaken: by + a past year → past perfect.

7while(see above)
8had overtaken(see above)

Part B · the complete Band 6 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

The line graph (9) illustrates how many hours per week young people aged 16 to 24 in one country spent on three leisure activities between 2005 and 2025.

Overall, the time spent on social media rose dramatically, and it overtook TV as the most popular activity. In (10) contrast, TV viewing fell steadily, (11) while reading was the least popular activity for most of the period.

In 2005, young people spent 16 hours a week watching TV, compared (12) with only 2 hours on social media. However, social media use increased (13) steadily to 11 hours in 2015, and it overtook TV shortly afterwards. By 2025, the figure had risen (14) to 18 hours. TV viewing, on the other hand, declined (15) by more than half over the period, (16) reaching only 7 hours in 2025.

Reading took up relatively little time throughout the period. It (17) decreased gradually from 6 hours in 2005 to 4 hours in 2015 and then remained stable at this (18) level until 2025. In 2025, young people spent more than four times (19) as much time on social media as on reading, while the (20) difference between reading and TV became much smaller.

Why this is a Band 6 answer

  • ✔ A clear overview: the main trends, and the fact that social media overtook TV.
  • ✔ Trend language with adverbs: rose dramatically, fell steadily, decreased gradually, remained stable.
  • ✔ Each point is supported with data and comparisons (compared with, more than four times as much … as).
  • ✔ A mix of tenses: past simple and past perfect (By 2025, the figure had risen …).
  • ✘ The vocabulary is good but fairly common, and several sentences follow the same pattern.
  • To reach Band 7: group the information more clearly and use more precise, less common words — look at the Band 7 sample.
W2 Writing · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1The figure for Japan was higher than that for Korea.

the figure for + a country or group. Compare like with like: than that for Korea (not than Korea).

2In 2015, TV was overtaken by streaming.

Passive = be + past participle: was overtaken (overtake – overtook – overtaken).

3Sales in 2020 were three times as high as in 2000.

three times as high as (as + adjective + as). With a comparative, use than: three times higher than.

4just under half

49% = just under half; 51% = just over half; 33% = roughly a third. Approximations make a report easier to read, but they must be accurate.

5The figures for cars and buses were 60% and 25% respectively.

respectively goes at the end: the first number belongs to the first item, the second number to the second item.

6There was a dramatic fall in prices.

adjective + noun: a dramatic fall in prices. (Or verb + adverb: Prices fell dramatically.)

7Overall, there was a clear shift from shopping in stores to shopping online, although stores still accounted for most sales.

A Band 7 overview sums up the main trend and the key comparison without detailed figures. The first option is a list of data; the third gives an opinion and a prediction that are not in the graph.

8Between 2005 and 2015, the figure doubled.

A finished period in the past → past simple (doubled). The present perfect needs a link to now, and the passive (was doubled) means that someone doubled it.

Part B · the complete Band 7 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

The line graph illustrates how much time young people aged 16 to 24 in one country (9) devoted to three leisure activities each week between 2005 and 2025.

Overall, the most (10) striking trend was the dramatic rise in the time spent on social media, which replaced television as the (11) dominant pastime. Television viewing declined (12) consistently throughout the period, (13) whereas reading changed relatively little and was the least popular activity from 2010 onwards.

In 2005, young people spent 16 hours a week watching television, eight times the figure for social media. (14) However, this gap narrowed rapidly as social media use (15) surged to 11 hours in 2015, and it overtook television shortly afterwards. By 2025, the figure had climbed to 18 hours, nine times its 2005 level. Television viewing, (16) meanwhile, fell steadily to just 7 hours, less than half of its (17) original figure.

Reading, by contrast, showed little (18) variation. The time spent reading for pleasure fell (19) gradually from 6 to 4 hours between 2005 and 2015 and then (20) levelled off for the rest of the period.

Why this is a Band 7 answer

  • ✔ A clear overview that picks out the key features: social media replaced TV, and reading stayed low and changed little.
  • ✔ Logical grouping: the two lines that crossed are described together, then reading.
  • ✔ Precise, less common vocabulary: devoted, striking, dominant pastime, surged, levelled off, variation.
  • ✔ A range of structures: whereas …, as social media use surged …, eight times the figure for …, nine times its 2005 level.
  • To reach Band 8: keep this accuracy and add even sharper comparisons, with no slips at all.

Speaking

W2 Speaking · Easy (Band 5–5.5)
QAnswerWhy
1per·CEN·tage

per·CEN·tage, like per·CENT: a high percentage, twenty percent.

2two thousand and six

From 2000 to 2009: two thousand and one … nine. From 2010 you can also say twenty ten, twenty twenty.

3two point five million

English uses a point (.) for decimals: 2.5 = two point five. (Vietnamese uses a comma: 2,5 triệu.)

4jumped

After p, k, s, f, sh, ch: -ed = /t/ → jumped /dʒʌmpt/. climbed and levelled end in /d/.

5When I was a child, I read a lot of comics, like Doraemon.

A past question needs the past tense: read (said /red/). Then add a detail (like Doraemon).

6I like reading books.

like + -ing (or like + to + verb): I like reading / I like to read.

7Every day — I use it for my studies and to watch videos.

How often needs a frequency: every day, a few times a week, once a month.

8My hometown has changed a lot.

has + past participle (has changed) for changes up to now.

9computer

com·PU·ter, but IN·ter·net and POP·u·lar.

10Paper books, because I like the feel of the pages.

Choose one, then give a reason with because.

11There are more cars in my city than before.

more … than before. Vietnamese “có” → there are, not there have.

12seventy-five percent

percent never takes -s: seventy-five percent.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Do you like reading?
Yes, I do. I usually read comics or short stories before I go to bed. It helps me relax.

How often do you use the internet?
Every day. I use it for my studies, and in the evening I watch videos on YouTube.

Has your hometown changed much?
Yes, it has. There are more cars and shops than before, and there is a new park near my house.

Do you prefer paper books or e-books?
I prefer paper books, because I like the feel of the pages. Reading on a screen makes my eyes tired.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you say the endings (-s, -ed) clearly?

W2 Speaking · Medium (Band 6–6.5)
QAnswerWhy
1Coffee is Vietnam’s biggest export.

Noun = EX·port (an export); verb = ex·PORT (to export). Many two-syllable words work like this: a RE·cord / to re·CORD.

2climbed

After voiced sounds (b, g, l, m, n, v, vowels): /d/ → climbed /klaɪmd/. After p: /t/ → jumped, dipped.

3three point two five million

After the point, say each digit separately: 3.25 = three point two five.

4Yes, quite a lot. There used to be rice fields everywhere, but now there are factories and new apartment blocks.

Past → present: There used to be … but now there are …

5I read much more than I used to.

much / far / a lot + comparative: much more, far more. Not very more.

6Mostly detective novels — I love trying to guess who did it before the end.

Answer the question (what kind?), then add a reason or a detail.

7I’m on my phone pretty much all day.

be on your phone = use it; pretty much = almost. Natural and informal — fine for Speaking.

8important

im·POR·tant, but IN·ter·est·ing and COMF·ta·ble (often said with 3 syllables).

9I’d say they read just as much, but in a different way — mostly short posts and articles on their phones.

A clear opinion (I’d say …), then a contrast with but.

10twenty seventeen

twenty seventeen (or two thousand and seventeen). The other options are not used.

11The number of tourists in my city has risen sharply.

rise – rose – risen. raise needs an object (raise prices).

12Yes, I used to read every night, but these days I’m so busy that I mostly read on the bus.

used to (past habit) → these days (present): the PPF idea from Week 1 (Past → Present → Future).

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Did you read a lot when you were a child?
Yes, I used to read every night before bed — mostly comics like Doraemon. These days I’m so busy that I mostly read on the bus.

Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
Quite a lot, actually. There used to be rice fields everywhere, but now there are factories and new apartment blocks, so the traffic is much heavier than before.

How much time do you spend on your phone?
Probably too much, to be honest — about five hours a day. I’m trying to cut down by leaving it in another room when I study.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you say the endings (-s, -ed) clearly?

Sample answers — practise saying them aloud

W2 Speaking · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)
QAnswerWhy
1economic

e·CON·o·my and e·CON·o·mist, but e·co·NOM·ic. In word families the stress often moves.

2a record / to record

a RE·cord (noun), to re·CORD (verb). Picture and visit keep the same stress.

3lasted

Only after t or d: last·ed /ɪd/. peaked = /t/ and plunged = /d/: still one syllable.

4I love reading.

A bookworm loves reading. Natural idioms like this help Lexical Resource.

5Probably less, if I’m honest. As a teenager I’d get through a novel a week, whereas now I mostly skim articles on my phone.

A natural opener, past vs present (I’d get through … whereas now …) and a specific detail. The last answer sounds memorised.

6I’ve read far more since I started taking the train to work.

Main clause: present perfect (I’ve read); after since: past simple (since I started). far + comparative (far more), not far much more.

7My neighbourhood has changed beyond recognition.

change beyond recognition = change so much that you cannot recognise it.

8a book so exciting that you can’t stop reading it

The new thriller is a real page-turner — I finished it in one night.

9Massively. Most people I know read on their phones now, which is convenient, but I think it makes us skim rather than read deeply.

A strong one-word opener, a detail and a balanced view (which is convenient, but …). In my opinion, I think says the same thing twice.

10“a lotta” /əˈlɒtə/

of becomes /ə/ before a consonant: a lotta people, kinda (kind of). Recognise it when you listen; you do not have to say it.

11nearly three quarters

74% is almost 75% = nearly three quarters. Useful in Speaking and in Writing Task 1.

12Absolutely. It’s probably the best way to build their vocabulary, and it gets them away from screens for a while.

Direct, with two clear reasons. The second answer just repeats the question; the third is far too formal for Part 1.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Do you read more now than when you were younger?
Probably less, if I’m honest. As a teenager I’d get through a novel a week, whereas now I mostly skim articles on my phone on the way to work.

How has technology changed the way people read?
Massively. Most people I know read on their phones now, which is convenient, but I think it encourages us to skim rather than read deeply.

Has your neighbourhood changed much?
It’s changed beyond recognition. When I was a kid it was mostly small family-run shops, but now it’s full of high-rise apartments and chain coffee shops.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you say the endings (-s, -ed) clearly?

WEEK 3

Listening + Writing

Listening Part 2: maps, plans and multiple-choice traps · Writing Task 2: question types, thesis and essay plan

This week you will
  • label a map or a floor plan in Listening Part 2: follow the speaker’s route and the direction words (opposite, next to, north of, at the end of …)
  • avoid multiple-choice traps: every option is mentioned, but only one answers the question
  • analyse a Writing Task 2 question, write a clear thesis statement and plan a four-paragraph essay
Practice audio
  • Warm-up: directions
  • Class practice: Glenview Campsite (map)
  • Class practice: multiple-choice traps
Common mistakes Vietnamese learners make

Listening

  • Reading the map from where you sit — start at the entrance (You are here) and follow the speaker
  • Choosing the first place you hear: wait for “It used to be … but now …”
  • Forgetting the compass: check where north is before you listen
  • Panicking after a missed answer — find the next labelled place and move on
  • Multiple choice: picking an option just because you heard its words

Writing

  • No clear position until the conclusion — put a thesis in the introduction
  • In my opinion, I think … → In my opinion, … or I believe …
  • Writing about the topic, not the question: answer every part of the task
  • Although …, but … → Although …, … (no but)
  • A new idea in the conclusion — sum up your position instead

Your daily 15-minute listening habit
  1. Listen once to a short clip (3–5 minutes) without the script. What is it about?
