Listening · Easy — Ashby Park

Practice test, week three. Listening, Part 2. Easy level.

You will hear the manager of Ashby Park talking to a group of local people about the changes to the park. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

Park manager (Tom): Good morning, everyone, and welcome back to Ashby Park. My name's Tom, and I'm the park manager.

Park manager (Tom): As you know, the park was closed for six months while we made some big changes. So today I'd like to tell you where everything is now. Please look at your map.

Park manager (Tom): We're standing at the main gate, on Park Road. That's at the bottom of your map.

Park manager (Tom): Let's start with the café. The old café was in the small building on the left, next to the car park. That building is now the park office.

Park manager (Tom): The new café is in the building on your right, just inside the main gate. It's much bigger, and it has lots of tables outside.

Park manager (Tom): Now, if you walk straight up the main path towards the lake, you'll come to the new children's playground. It's next to the main path, on the left, just before you get to the lake.

Park manager (Tom): There's a fence all round it, so small children can't run down to the water.

Park manager (Tom): Next, the toilets. The old toilets were in the corner of the park, near Park Road, on the right. We've knocked them down, and that corner is now a place to leave your bicycle.

Park manager (Tom): The new toilets are on the east side of the lake, near the trees along the fence.

Park manager (Tom): Now, our famous rose garden. It hasn't moved. It's still on the west side of the park, between the car park and the tennis courts.

Park manager (Tom): And finally, the picnic area. Lots of people like to have a picnic on the grass near the café, and that's fine. But if you'd like a table, go to the picnic area.

Park manager (Tom): We've put twenty new picnic tables there. You'll find it on the north side of the lake, at the top of your map.

Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

Park manager (Tom): Now, some information about using the park. First, the café. Many of you will remember that the old café was always closed on Mondays.

Park manager (Tom): Well, the new café is open every day, from eight in the morning until six in the evening. The ice-cream kiosk by the lake is different. That's only open at weekends.

Park manager (Tom): Dogs are still very welcome in the park. Some people asked us to keep dogs out of the rose garden, but we decided not to do that.

Park manager (Tom): You don't need to keep your dog on a lead in most parts of the park. But please keep dogs on a lead near the playground. That's a new rule.

Park manager (Tom): Next, the tennis courts. In the past, you booked a court by phone or at the park office. Now you can only book online, on the park website.

Park manager (Tom): We've got some events coming up, too. Last summer we had a flower show in the rose garden, and next month there's a concert by the lake.

Park manager (Tom): But this Saturday there's a fun run round the lake. It starts at ten o'clock, and everyone is welcome.

Park manager (Tom): One last thing. There are lots of new rubbish bins, so you don't need to take your rubbish home. And the car park is still free.

Park manager (Tom): But please don't feed the ducks on the lake. Bread is very bad for them.

Park manager (Tom): Thank you for listening. Enjoy the new park!

That is the end of Part 2.

Listening · Medium — Harbour Arts Centre

Practice test, week three. Listening, Part 2. Medium level.

You will hear a guide talking to visitors at the start of an open day at the Harbour Arts Centre. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

Guide (Grace): Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Arts Centre open day. I'm Grace, and I'm one of the guides here.

Guide (Grace): Before we look round, let me tell you a little about the building. Because we're right next to the harbour, people often assume it was a fish market. In fact, the fish market was on the other side of the harbour.

Guide (Grace): There were boatyards along this street, too, but this building was built as a warehouse, for storing tea and coffee that arrived by ship.

Guide (Grace): It became an arts centre in 1995, and since then we've made a lot of improvements. The question visitors ask most is whether we're going to open a cinema. Sadly, we simply haven't got the space.

Guide (Grace): The big news this year is that we've put in a lift, so every floor is now open to wheelchair users and people with pushchairs. And the rooftop terrace you may have read about should open next summer.

Guide (Grace): Now, our classes. We used to run all our adult classes on Saturday mornings. Then we tried weekday mornings, but hardly anyone came, because most of our students work.

Guide (Grace): So adult classes now take place on weekday evenings, after work. Saturday mornings are for our family workshops.

Guide (Grace): A quick word about prices. The full guided tour of the building costs three pounds, and I'm afraid the car park behind the centre belongs to the council, so you'll have to pay there too.

Guide (Grace): But the photography exhibition on the ground floor is completely free, so please do have a look.

Guide (Grace): Finally, a few rules. You're welcome to take photographs anywhere in the building, as long as you don't use a flash. And your phones are fine, as long as they're on silent.

Guide (Grace): But we do ask you to leave large bags in the cloakroom. They can easily knock things over in the galleries.

Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

Guide (Grace): Right. If you look at the plan of the ground floor, you'll see that we're standing at reception, just inside the main entrance.

Guide (Grace): Let's start with the cloakroom, as I've just mentioned it. Some of you may remember that it used to be on the right as you came in.

Guide (Grace): It's now the room immediately on your left as you come through the entrance, next to the stairs.

Guide (Grace): The room on the other side, where the cloakroom used to be, is now our gift shop. So that's the room immediately on your right, next to the lift. It sells cards and prints by local artists.

Guide (Grace): Now, if you walk past reception, you come to the corridor that runs across the building. Turn left, and the first room on your right is the dance studio.

The Social Life of Public Spaces

A  In the 1960s, many of the new office towers in New York City were built with open plazas at their base. The city’s 1961 zoning rules encouraged this: developers were not obliged to provide a plaza, but those who did were allowed to build extra floor space. Yet many of the new plazas were little used. Why did some public spaces attract crowds while others stood almost empty?

In simple English: New York’s 1961 rules gave developers extra floor space for building a plaza, but many of the new plazas were little used. Why?

B  One person who set out to answer this question was William H. Whyte, a journalist best known for his 1956 bestseller The Organization Man. In 1969, while helping the city’s Planning Commission with a plan for New York, Whyte began to wonder whether the new plazas actually worked, and the following year he formed a small research group, the Street Life Project. Rather than simply asking people what they wanted, Whyte and his assistants watched what they did. They filmed plazas with time-lapse cameras and noted where people sat, stood and talked. The results were presented in 1980 in a book and a film, both called The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces.

In simple English: William H. Whyte’s Street Life Project (from 1970) watched and filmed how people used plazas instead of asking them; the results came out in 1980.

Tiếng Việt: Dự án Street Life của William H. Whyte (từ năm 1970) quan sát và quay phim cách mọi người dùng quảng trường thay vì hỏi họ; kết quả được công bố năm 1980 (sách và phim).

C  Some of the findings seemed almost too obvious to state. Features that designers might expect to matter, such as the size or shape of a plaza, turned out to matter less than one simple factor. As Whyte put it, “People tend to sit most where there are places to sit.” The most popular spaces offered plenty of seating of many kinds: benches, steps and wide ledges. Whyte was especially enthusiastic about movable chairs, because they let people decide for themselves where to sit — in the sun or in the shade, alone or in a group. He noticed that people often moved a chair a few inches before sitting down, even when it ended up almost where it had been.

In simple English: The key factor was seating: people sit where there are places to sit. Movable chairs are popular because people can choose where to sit.

Tiếng Việt: Yếu tố quan trọng nhất là chỗ ngồi: người ta ngồi ở nơi có chỗ để ngồi. Ghế di động được ưa thích vì mỗi người có thể tự chọn chỗ (nắng hay râm, một mình hay theo nhóm) — người ta thường xê dịch ghế một chút trước khi ngồi.

D  A second key finding concerned other people. Whyte’s films showed that people did not, as many designers assumed, seek out quiet corners away from the crowd. Instead, they tended to stop and talk in the middle of the busiest flows of pedestrians, often near street corners and the entrances of buildings. “What attracts people most, it would appear, is other people,” Whyte concluded. He also described a process he called “triangulation”, in which something external — a street performer, say, or an unusual sculpture — gives strangers a reason to start talking to each other.

In simple English: People are attracted by other people: they stop to talk in the busiest places, and “triangulation” (a performer or a sculpture) gets strangers talking.

E  Whyte’s research had practical consequences. In simple English: Whyte’s ideas shaped New York’s 1975 plaza rules (seating, trees), the Project for Public Spaces and the restoration of Bryant Park (1988–1992): the tall hedges went, the entrances were opened up and movable chairs were added.

His book Life Between Buildings, first published in 1971, argued that architects and planners should pay close attention to the life that takes place in the spaces between buildings, not just to the buildings themselves.

In simple English: In Copenhagen, Strøget was closed to cars in 1962, and Jan Gehl studied how people used it; his 1971 book focused on the life between buildings.

Tiếng Việt: Ở Copenhagen, phố Strøget cấm ô tô từ năm 1962 (ban đầu chỉ là thử nghiệm); kiến trúc sư Jan Gehl nghiên cứu cách người dân sử dụng nó, và cuốn sách năm 1971 của ông nhấn mạnh “cuộc sống giữa các tòa nhà”.

G  The lessons of this research may seem like common sense, yet they are still often ignored: it is not hard to find new plazas that look impressive in an architect’s drawing but offer nowhere comfortable to sit. Whyte’s work suggests that the success of a public space depends less on how it looks than on how well it supports the ordinary things people like to do: sitting, watching, meeting and talking.

In simple English: These lessons are still often ignored: a public space succeeds when it supports what people like to do — sit, watch, meet and talk.

Tiếng Việt: Những bài học này vẫn thường bị bỏ qua: một không gian công cộng thành công khi nó phục vụ những việc người ta thích làm — ngồi, ngắm, gặp gỡ và trò chuyện.

Writing

The task (the same at every level)

Writing Task 2: Some people believe that city councils should spend more money on parks and other public spaces. Others think that this money would be better spent on housing and public transport. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

W3 Writing · Easy (Band 5–5.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1a discussion question

Discuss both views and give your own opinion = a discussion question: write about both views, and say what you think. (An opinion question asks To what extent do you agree or disagree?; a problem and solution question asks about causes or problems and solutions.)

2the problems and the solutions

Problem and solution questions have two parts: the problems (or causes) and the solutions. Answer both.

3Although parks are important, I believe that housing and public transport should come first.

A thesis statement gives your position clearly. The second option has no opinion; the third one is long, but it does not choose — and In my opinion, I think says the same thing twice.

4Intro: both views + my opinion · Body 1: why parks are important · Body 2: why housing and transport are important · Conclusion: my opinion again

A discussion essay needs both views (one in each body paragraph) and your opinion — in the introduction and again in the conclusion. The other plans are about the topic, but they do not answer the question.

5Nowadays, many people think that parks are important.

people is plural → people think. Never are think: be + a verb is not a tense.

6Although parks are useful, they are expensive.

Although …, … — no but (Vietnamese Mặc dù … nhưng …). Or: Parks are useful, but they are expensive.

7The government should build more homes.

should / can / must + the base verb: should build.

8Children need places to play.

child → children (already plural: no -s) → children need.

Part B · the complete Band 5 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

Nowadays, many cities (9) have to decide how to spend their money. Some people think that city councils should (10) spend more money on parks and public spaces, but (11) other people think that housing and public transport are more important. I think that housing and public transport should come first.

On the one (12) hand, parks are very important for people in cities. People can go to the park to (13) relax and do exercise after work. Children can play there (14) safely, and old people can meet their friends. Parks also have many trees, so the air is (15) cleaner. Parks are also free, so poor families can use them too. For example, in my city there is a big park near the lake, and many people go there every morning to walk or play badminton.

On the other hand, housing and public transport are also very important. In big cities, houses are very expensive, (16) so many young people cannot buy a house. If the council (17) builds more cheap houses, these people will have a place to live. Public transport is important too, (18) because many people travel to work by bus. For example, my cousin lives far from his office, and he spends two hours on the bus every day. If there are more buses, there will be (19) less traffic and cleaner air.

In (20) conclusion, I think that both are important, but housing and public transport are more important than parks. People need a home and a way to get to work first. However, the council should not forget about parks completely.

Why this is a Band 5 answer

  • ✔ It answers both parts of the task: both views and the writer’s own opinion (in the introduction and again in the conclusion).
  • ✔ Clear paragraphs: an introduction, one paragraph for each view and a conclusion.
  • ✔ Simple linking words are used correctly (On the one hand, On the other hand, because, so, In conclusion).
  • ✘ The ideas are listed rather than developed: each reason gets one short sentence, and the examples are very simple.
  • ✘ The vocabulary is basic and repeated (important again and again), and most sentences are short and simple.
  • To reach Band 6: develop each idea with a reason and an example, and use a wider range of words and sentence types — look at the Band 6 sample.
W3 Writing · Medium (Band 6–6.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1Give your own opinion on free public transport and support it.

To what extent do you agree or disagree? = an opinion essay: say how much you agree, and keep the same position from the introduction to the conclusion. Discussing both views equally is what a discussion question asks for (Discuss both views and give your own opinion), not an opinion question.

2City councils have to decide how to spend limited budgets. While some people would put parks first, others think housing and transport matter more; in my view, housing and transport should come first.

The best introduction paraphrases the question and gives a thesis. The third option copies the question (copied words do not count), and the first is only about parks and has no position.

3Supporters of spending on parks argue that green spaces improve people’s health and quality of life.

A topic sentence tells the reader the main idea of the paragraph. The second option only announces a list of topics; the third is an example, not the main idea — it could come later in the paragraph, after the topic sentence.

4Body 1: the benefits of parks · Body 2: why housing and transport matter more · Conclusion: housing and transport first, ideally with small parks

A discussion essay needs both views and a clear opinion. The second plan gives only one view; the third is about the topic, not the question.

5Councils should spend more money on parks.

spend money on something (and spend time doing something).

6Although

Although + a clause (despite / because of + a noun) · who for people · However, starts a new sentence and needs a comma.

7who(see above)
8However(see above)

Part B · the complete Band 6 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

Nowadays, many city councils have a limited budget, so they must decide what to (9) spend their money on. (10) While some people think that parks and public spaces need more money, others believe that housing and public transport should (11) come first. In my opinion, housing and transport are more important, but parks should not be (12) ignored.

Firstly, people who support spending on parks point (13) out that green spaces are good for people’s health. In big cities, a park is often the only place (14) where people can do exercise, relax or meet their friends. Trees also (15) reduce air pollution and make the streets cooler in summer. In Hanoi, (16) for instance, the parks are full of people doing exercise early in the morning. Because of these benefits, many people want councils to build more parks.

Secondly, there are also good reasons to put housing and transport first. House prices and rents in many cities have (17) risen very quickly, so young people and poor families (18) struggle to find a good place to live. For example, many young workers have to share a small room with other people. Cheaper homes would meet a basic need that a park cannot meet. (19) Similarly, a cheap and reliable bus or metro system meets another basic need: it allows people to travel to work and school, and it also reduces traffic jams.

In conclusion, although parks are useful for city residents, I believe that councils should spend more money on housing and public transport, because these meet people’s most basic needs. (20) Ideally, new housing projects should also include small parks, so that both goals can be achieved.

Why this is a Band 6 answer

  • ✔ A clear position in the introduction (In my opinion, …), repeated in the conclusion.
  • ✔ Both views are discussed in separate paragraphs, each with reasons and an example.
  • ✔ Linking words are used correctly (While, Similarly, for instance, although), but some are mechanical (Firstly, Secondly).
  • ✘ Some points are listed rather than explained (why exactly are parks good for health?), and the examples are short.
  • ✘ The vocabulary is clear but simple and repeated (good, cheap, important, basic need).
  • To reach Band 7: develop each main idea more fully and use more precise vocabulary and complex sentences — look at the Band 7 sample.
W3 Writing · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)

Part A

QAnswerWhy
1While green spaces undoubtedly improve city life, I would argue that affordable housing and efficient transport are more urgent priorities for council spending.

The third option states a clear position, previews the reason (urgency) and recognises the other view. The first is over-hedged: it never takes a position. The second takes a position but ignores the other view completely (the only things), although the task asks you to discuss both views.

2Parks should be closed at night so that they stay clean and safe.

Every sentence must help to answer the question (Task Response). The second sentence is about parks, but it is about how parks should be run — not about whether councils should spend more money on parks or on housing and transport.

3In conclusion, while parks have real benefits, housing and transport meet more basic needs, so they deserve a larger share of council budgets.

A good conclusion restates your position and sums up the main reason. The second adds a new argument (house prices) that the essay never developed; the third suddenly gives up the position of the introduction.

4in the introduction and the conclusion (it can also be developed in a body paragraph)

The task asks for your opinion, and a Band 7 essay keeps a clear position throughout: state it in the thesis and repeat it in the conclusion.

5Not only do parks improve health, but they also bring people together.

Not only at the start of a sentence → question word order: Not only do parks improve …, but they also …

6A large amount of money is spent on roads.

an amount of + an uncountable noun (money, time, traffic) + a singular verb; a number of + a plural noun (cars, parks).

7Investing in housing would benefit the whole city.

A verb as the subject of a sentence → -ing (a gerund): Investing in housing …

8Parks and transport both matter: the former improves health, while the latter helps people reach their jobs.

the former = the first thing mentioned (parks); the latter = the second (transport). They never take -s.

Part B · the complete Band 7 sample answer (the missing words are highlighted)

As cities grow, councils face (9) increasingly difficult choices about how to (10) allocate limited public funds. Some argue that parks and other shared spaces should be a priority, whereas others (11) maintain that the money would be better (12) invested in housing and public transport. While I recognise the value of green space, I believe that housing and transport are more (13) pressing concerns.

Advocates of investment in public spaces argue that such spaces are (14) essential to urban well-being. Parks, squares and riverside paths offer free places for exercise and relaxation, which can reduce stress and improve public health, (15) particularly for residents of small apartments with no outdoor space. In many Asian cities, parks are crowded at dawn with people jogging, dancing or practising tai chi, which shows how much such spaces are valued. (16) Moreover, well-designed public spaces bring together people from (17) different backgrounds, strengthening a sense of community that is often missing in large cities.

(18) Nevertheless, the case for prioritising housing and transport is, in my view, stronger. A shortage of (19) affordable homes forces many young workers and low-income families either to spend a large proportion of their income on rent or to move far from the city centre. Efficient public transport (20) addresses the second problem directly: it connects these residents to jobs and services, and it reduces the congestion and pollution that affect everyone. Without these basic foundations, even the most attractive park cannot significantly improve people’s lives.

In conclusion, although public spaces undoubtedly enhance city life, councils should focus first on providing affordable housing and reliable transport. The most effective approach, however, may be to combine housing and green space by requiring every new development to include an accessible park.

Why this is a Band 7 answer

  • ✔ A clear, balanced position from the first paragraph (While I recognise …, I believe …), kept to the end.
  • ✔ Each body paragraph has a clear topic sentence, developed with reasons and consequences.
  • ✔ Precise vocabulary: allocate, pressing concerns, advocates, affordable, congestion.
  • ✔ A range of complex structures: whereas …, which can …, either … or …, Without these basic foundations, …
  • To reach Band 8: support each view with a specific, well-chosen example and keep the same accuracy throughout.

Speaking

W3 Speaking · Easy (Band 5–5.5)
QAnswerWhy
1LI·brar·y

LI·brar·y /ˈlaɪ.brər.i/: the stress is on the first syllable.

2museum

mu·SE·um /mjuːˈziː.əm/, but CIN·e·ma and RES·tau·rant.

3It’s a small city in the north of Vietnam, about two hours from Hanoi.

Give the place and one useful detail: in the north of Vietnam, about two hours from Hanoi. Never say Vietnam country, and not where is (→ which is).

4My neighbourhood is very quiet.

An English sentence needs a verb: is + an adjective (quiet). Vietnamese often has no verb here (Khu tôi rất yên tĩnh).

5Go straight on and take the second turning on the left. It’s opposite the bank.

Directions use the base verb: Go straight on, take the second turning. Finish with a landmark: opposite the bank (not opposite with; not must to).

6I live in a quiet area near the city centre.

live in an area / a city / a district; at + an address: at 25 Le Loi Street.

7It’s really quiet, but there are still lots of shops nearby.

Answer the question, then add a detail. The first answer is long, but it has mistakes: many shops, the people are.

8three

NEIGH·bour·hood /ˈneɪ.bə.hʊd/ — three syllables, stressed on the first.

9Yes, there’s a small one about five minutes’ walk from my house.

there’s a + a noun, then a detail (five minutes’ walk). Vietnamese có → there is / there are, not have.

10I have lived here since 2015.

From the past until now + since → the present perfect: I have lived here since 2015.

11HOS·pi·tal

HOS·pi·tal /ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl/.

12Yes, I’d love to, because there are more jobs and more things to do.

I’d love to (= I would love to live there) + a reason with because. Not would like to living, and many job opportunities.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Where is your hometown?
It’s a small city in the north of Vietnam, about two hours from Hanoi. It’s famous for its rice fields and its old temples.

Do you like your neighbourhood?
Yes, I do. It’s quiet, but it’s close to the market and my children’s school, so it’s very convenient.

Is there anything you would like to change about your area?
I’d like more trees and a park, because at the moment there isn’t anywhere green for children to play.

How do you usually get around?
I usually go by motorbike. It’s quick and cheap, but it’s not much fun in the rain.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you stress the place words correctly, and did you add a detail or a reason?

Sample answers — practise saying them aloud

W3 Speaking · Medium (Band 6–6.5)
QAnswerWhy
1hotel

ho·TEL /həʊˈtel/, but CIN·e·ma and SU·per·mar·ket.

2cathedral

ca·THE·dral /kəˈθiː.drəl/, but THEA·tre and STA·di·um.

3Yes, quite a lot. They’ve built a new shopping centre, so it’s much busier than it used to be.

The present perfect for changes up to now (They’ve built), then a comparison with the past: busier than it used to be. Yes, it has. is correct but far too short; the third answer has a mistake (is building).

4Keep going until you get to the traffic lights, and then turn right.

Keep going until you get to … + a landmark, then turn right (the base verb, no direction).

5By motorbike, probably. The buses are cheap, but they’re quite slow and often crowded.

A direct answer (By motorbike, probably) + a comparison with another option (The buses are cheap, but …). The first answer has mistakes (by the motorbike, more faster); the second is a memorised sentence that does not answer the question.

6It takes about twenty minutes to get to the city centre.

It takes + time + to + a verb. People spend time; a journey takes time.

7far from the places most tourists visit

My village is a bit off the beaten track = quiet, away from the usual tourist places.

8Not really, to be honest. Everyone’s so busy that we just say hello in the lift.

Not really, to be honest is a natural opener; then explain why. Yes, I do. is correct but too short, and the second answer does not answer the question.

9There’s a lot of traffic in my area.

traffic is uncountable: a lot of traffic, heavy traffic — never traffics.

10the first part: BUS station, POST office

Most compound nouns are stressed on the first part: BUS station, POST office, SHOPping centre. (A few place names are different: city CENtre, town HALL.)

11Definitely — especially in autumn, when the weather’s cooler and there are lots of festivals.

A strong opener (Definitely) + especially + a detail. The first answer has mistakes: there are many famous places (not there have), I’d recommend it. The third sounds memorised and gives no real detail.

12My hometown has become much more crowded than before.

has + become (become – became – become).

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
Quite a lot, actually. They’ve built a new shopping centre and a ring road, so it’s much busier than it used to be — though the traffic’s got worse too.

What’s the best way to get around your city?
By motorbike, probably. The buses are cheap and air-conditioned, but they’re slow, and you never quite know when they’ll come.

Do you know your neighbours well?
Not really, to be honest. Everyone in my building works long hours, so we mostly just say hello in the lift.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you stress the place words correctly, and did you add a detail or a reason?

Sample answers — practise saying them aloud

W3 Speaking · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)
QAnswerWhy
1entertainment

en·ter·TAIN·ment /ˌen.təˈteɪn.mənt/; AR·chi·tec·ture; ac·com·mo·DA·tion (the fourth syllable).

2photograph → photography

PHO·to·graph → pho·TOG·ra·phy. The other pairs keep the stress on the first syllable.

3It is full of tall buildings and has very little green space.

a concrete jungle = a city area full of big buildings and few trees — usually negative.

4It’s been completely transformed — most of the old street stalls have been replaced by trendy cafés, which is a mixed blessing, really.

Natural, precise language (transformed, replaced by, a mixed blessing) and a personal view. The third answer uses long words, but it is over-formal, sounds memorised and gives no real detail.

5If they hadn’t built the metro line, the traffic would be even worse now.

A mixed conditional: a past cause (hadn’t built) → a present result (would be … now).

6Sorry, I’m not from round here — but there’s a map just outside the station.

Apologise, give the reason (I’m not from round here) and offer some help. The first reply is over-formal for the street; Sorry, I don’t know. is natural but does not help.

7very close to

My flat is a stone’s throw from the beach = very close to it.

8The traffic is very heavy in the city centre at rush hour.

heavy traffic / the traffic is heavy. Roads are busy or congested (not heavy), and crowded is for places (crowded streets, a crowded bus), not for traffic.

9There used to be a cinema where the bank is now.

There used to be + a noun for things that existed in the past. Vietnamese có → there was / there used to be, not there used to have.

10To some extent. There’s plenty going on at weekends, but there aren’t many well-paid jobs, so a lot of my friends have moved to Ho Chi Minh City.

A hedged answer (To some extent), both sides (but …) and a real example. The first answer is over-formal and sounds memorised; the third is natural but gives no reason or example.

11joined together: each final consonant links to the next vowel (live‿in‿an‿old)

Consonant → vowel linking makes your speech smoother: li-vi-na-nold.

12The suburbs, I think. I’d happily put up with a longer commute in exchange for some peace and quiet and a bit of green space.

Choose one, then give a reason with natural phrases (put up with, in exchange for). would rather + the base verb, with no to; prefer A to B (not prefer … more than).

Now practise aloud: sample answers

How has your neighbourhood changed?
It’s been completely transformed. When I was a kid it was all street stalls and family-run shops; now it’s trendy cafés and high-rise apartments, which is a bit of a mixed blessing, really.

Is your hometown a good place for young people?
To some extent. There’s plenty going on at weekends, but there aren’t many well-paid jobs, so a lot of my friends have ended up moving to Ho Chi Minh City.

Would you rather live in the city centre or the suburbs?
The suburbs, I think. I’d happily put up with a longer commute in exchange for a bit of peace and quiet and some green space.

Read each sample answer aloud twice. Then answer the question yourself in 20–30 seconds and record yourself on your phone: did you stress the place words correctly, and did you add a detail or a reason?

WEEK 4

Reading + Speaking

Matching headings and matching information · Speaking Part 2: cue cards, the 1-minute plan and storytelling

This week you will
  • match headings to paragraphs: find the main idea of each paragraph and avoid the distractor headings
  • find which paragraph contains a piece of information by scanning for paraphrases
  • speak for two minutes in Speaking Part 2: read the cue card, make a 1-minute plan and tell a clear story in the past
Practice audio
  • Warm-up: say it another way
Common mistakes Vietnamese learners make

Reading

  • Choosing a heading because it has the same word as the paragraph — match the meaning
  • Choosing a heading from one detail or from the first sentence only (the main idea may come after However)
  • Using a heading twice — each heading is used only once
  • Matching information: expecting the answers in passage order, or thinking every letter must be used
  • Translating every word instead of skimming each paragraph for its main idea

Speaking

  • Stopping after one minute — keep talking until the examiner says “Thank you”
  • Writing full sentences in the 1-minute plan (key words only!)
  • Wrong past forms: I go / I buyed → I went / I bought
  • I was boring → I was bored (-ed = how you feel)
  • Forgetting the last point on the card: explain why…
Homework — choose your level for each skill
Skill Easy
Band 5–5.5		 Medium
Band 6–6.5		 Challenging
Band 7–7.5		 Time
Listening Easy Medium Challenging 10–15 min
Reading Easy Medium Challenging 20 min
Writing Easy Medium Challenging 20–30 min
Speaking Easy Medium Challenging 10–15 min

Which level should I choose? (Chọn mức độ nào?)

  • Easy (Band 5–5.5) — English is still hard for you, or you are new to IELTS.
  • Medium (Band 6–6.5) — your level is around Band 5.5–6.
  • Challenging (Band 7–7.5) — you are aiming for Band 7 or higher.
  • Want more practice? Do your level first, then try the next one.
Your daily 15-minute listening habit
  1. Listen once to a short clip (3–5 minutes) without the script. What is it about?
  2. Listen again with the transcript. Highlight the “dark areas” — the words you could not hear. Say them aloud.
  3. Shadow 3–5 sentences: play, pause, repeat with the same speed and rhythm.

Free sources: BBC Learning English (try 6 Minute English) · British Council LearnEnglish – Listening · TED-Ed

Bonus (optional): real exam practice

Cambridge IELTS 17 · Test 3 · Reading Passage 2 (matching information) and Test 4 · Speaking Part 2 (a cue card about a past occasion) — materials not included; use your own copy of the book.

Answers and explanations for all homework quizzes

How to use this page

Listening

W4 Listening · Easy (Band 5–5.5)
QAnswerReplayWhy

Listening · Easy — A city farm

Practice test, week four. Listening, Part 2. Easy level.

You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a city farm. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

Guide (Helen): Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook City Farm. My name's Helen, and I'm one of the guides here. Before you go and explore, I'm going to tell you about the different places you can visit on the farm today.

Guide (Helen): Let's start with the animal barn. That's the big red building just behind me. Inside, you can meet our goats, our sheep and two very friendly pigs. The barn is open all day, from nine until five. The animals love to eat, but please don't give them any of your own food, because it can make them ill. For the animals that share these spaces with us, cities are a strange new habitat: hotter than the surrounding countryside, brightly lit at night, noisy, polluted and cut into pieces by roads. Some species simply disappear as cities grow. Others survive and seem to change in response — and in a growing number of cases, biologists believe that they are watching evolution happen in real time.

In simple English: Most people now live in cities, which are a strange new habitat for animals. Some species disappear; others change — perhaps by evolving.

Tiếng Việt: Hơn một nửa dân số thế giới sống ở đô thị. Với động vật, thành phố là môi trường sống mới và lạ (nóng, sáng đèn ban đêm, ồn, ô nhiễm, bị đường sá chia cắt). Có loài biến mất, có loài thay đổi — có thể là đang tiến hóa.

B  The best-known example comes from nineteenth-century England. Peppered moths are normally pale with dark speckles, which hides them on lichen-covered tree bark. In 1848, however, a dark form was recorded in Manchester, and by 1895 around 98 per cent of the peppered moths in the area were reported to be dark. Factory smoke had killed the lichens and blackened the trees, so pale moths stood out to hungry birds while dark ones were hidden. Bernard Kettlewell’s experiments in the 1950s supported this explanation, although his methods were later criticised, and a larger study by Michael Majerus, published in 2012, three years after his death, confirmed that birds were the main cause. After Britain’s Clean Air Act of 1956, the dark form became rare again.

In simple English: The peppered moth is the classic example: pollution made dark moths safer from birds, and they became rare again after the air was cleaned.

Tiếng Việt: Bướm đêm Biston betularia là ví dụ kinh điển: khói nhà máy làm thân cây đen lại nên bướm màu sẫm khó bị chim phát hiện (đến 1895 khoảng 98% là bướm sẫm). Nghiên cứu sau này xác nhận nguyên nhân là chim ăn bướm; sau Luật Không khí sạch 1956, bướm sẫm lại trở nên hiếm.

C  Noise is another challenge. Many birds use song to attract a mate and defend a territory, but the low rumble of traffic can drown out their calls. In 2003, two Dutch researchers reported that great tits in the city of Leiden sang at a higher minimum pitch in noisier places. A later comparison of birds in ten European cities with birds in nearby forests found the same pattern: city songs were higher, shorter and faster, which may help them to be heard above low-pitched traffic noise. Birds can adjust their songs by learning, however, so the change is not necessarily genetic.

In simple English: City birds sing higher, shorter and faster songs, which may help them to be heard over traffic — but this may be learned, not genetic.

Tiếng Việt: Chim ở thành phố hót cao hơn, ngắn hơn và nhanh hơn chim ở rừng, có lẽ để át tiếng xe cộ trầm. Nhưng chim có thể học cách hót, nên thay đổi này chưa chắc là do gen.

D  Roads, too, can shape animals’ bodies. Since 1982, the biologists Charles and Mary Brown have studied cliff swallows that nest on bridges and overpasses in south-western Nebraska, in the United States. Over three decades, the number killed by passing cars fell from as many as twenty a year to only a handful, even though the number of nesting birds rose and traffic did not decrease. The birds killed on the roads had longer wings than the population as a whole, and the population’s average wing length had become shorter. Shorter wings may allow a steeper take-off, helping a bird to escape an oncoming car, although other factors may also have played a part.

In simple English: Cliff swallows near roads in Nebraska have evolved shorter wings, and far fewer are now killed by cars.

Tiếng Việt: Chim nhạn vách đá làm tổ dưới cầu ở bang Nebraska (Mỹ): sau 30 năm, số chim bị xe đâm giảm mạnh; chim bị đâm có cánh dài hơn, còn cánh trung bình của cả quần thể ngắn đi — có thể giúp cất cánh nhanh để tránh xe.

E  But is such a change genetic, or do animals simply adjust their behaviour or development? One way to find out is to raise them under identical conditions. In Puerto Rico, Kristin Winchell and her colleagues found that crested anoles — small lizards — living in cities had relatively longer limbs and more lamellae, the tiny scales on their toes that help them cling to smooth surfaces such as walls and metal fences. When the team raised the young of city and forest lizards in a laboratory, the offspring of city parents still had more lamellae and longer front legs, suggesting that the differences are inherited, and a genetic study published in 2023 supported this.

In simple English: City lizards in Puerto Rico have longer legs and more toe scales, and lab-raised young still have them, so the differences seem to be inherited.

Tiếng Việt: Thằn lằn ở thành phố Puerto Rico có chân dài hơn và nhiều vảy bám ở ngón chân hơn (bám tường, hàng rào kim loại). Con non nuôi trong phòng thí nghiệm vẫn có các đặc điểm đó → có thể là do di truyền.

F  Such careful testing matters, because many differences between urban and rural animals turn out not to be evolutionary at all. An animal may learn new behaviour, or its body may develop differently in a new environment, without any change in its genes — a flexibility that biologists call phenotypic plasticity. When a team led by Max Lambert reviewed 270 studies of urban evolution in 2021, they found strong evidence of genetic adaptation to city life in only six cases, one of which was the peppered moth.

In simple English: Many city–country differences are not evolution but flexibility (phenotypic plasticity); a review of 270 studies found strong evidence in only six cases.

Tiếng Việt: Nhiều khác biệt giữa động vật thành thị và nông thôn không phải do tiến hóa mà do khả năng thích nghi linh hoạt (học hỏi, phát triển khác đi). Một tổng quan 270 nghiên cứu chỉ thấy bằng chứng mạnh về tiến hóa ở 6 trường hợp.

G  None of this means that cities are good for wildlife; for many species, they are deadly. But they do offer biologists a remarkable opportunity. Because cities around the world share similar features — heat, light, noise and hard surfaces — they work like a series of repeated natural experiments, allowing researchers to test whether separate populations respond to the same pressures in the same way. As the Dutch biologist Menno Schilthuizen argues in his 2018 book Darwin Comes to Town, the urban jungle may be one of the best places to watch evolution at work.

In simple English: Cities are not good for wildlife, but because they are so similar, they work like natural laboratories for studying evolution.

Tiếng Việt: Thành phố không tốt cho động vật hoang dã, nhưng vì các thành phố trên thế giới giống nhau (nóng, sáng, ồn, bề mặt cứng), chúng giống như những “thí nghiệm tự nhiên” lặp lại — nơi lý tưởng để quan sát tiến hóa.

The task (the same at every level)

Writing Task 2: In many countries, a large amount of food is thrown away every day by households, shops and restaurants. Why does this happen? What can be done to solve this problem? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

Part A

QAnswerWhy

A topic sentence gives the main idea of the whole paragraph. The other two sentences are small details, and they do not introduce the paragraph.

When an action is the subject of a sentence, use the -ing form: Buying too much food is… Vietnamese “Mua quá nhiều thức ăn” has no -ing, so learners often write Buy too much food is….

A plural subject (many families) + do not. Never put not alone before a verb.

Use because or so — not both (Vietnamese “Vì… nên…”). because + subject + verb; because of + a noun (because of big meals).

Nowadays, a lot of food (9) is thrown away every day in many countries. This is a big problem, because many people in the world do not have enough food to eat. In this essay, I will explain why this happens and what we can do about it.

There are two main reasons for this problem. First, many families buy too much food at the supermarket, (10) so some of it goes bad before they can eat it. (11) For example, my aunt often buys a big bag of fruit, and half of the fruit (12) goes in the bin. Second, restaurants often give customers very big meals, because they want their customers to feel happy. Many people cannot finish (13) these meals, so the food is wasted. Also, when I eat at a restaurant with my friends, we often leave a lot of rice and meat on our plates.

(14) However, there are some solutions to this problem. Families should make a shopping list (15) because it helps them to buy only what they need. My mother writes a list every Sunday, so we waste less food now. In (16) addition, restaurants could offer smaller meals (17) at a lower price. Supermarkets can also give unsold food to people in need, for example through charities. This will help people, and it is (18) good for the environment, because there will be less rubbish.

In (19) conclusion, food waste happens (20) because of bad planning and very big meals in restaurants. I believe that families, restaurants and supermarkets can solve this problem together, and everyone should think carefully before they buy food.

In many countries, a surprising amount of food ends up in the bin, which wastes money and harms the environment. This essay will examine the main causes of this problem and suggest (9) some practical solutions.

The main reason is that many households buy more food than they need. Supermarkets encourage this with special offers (10) such as ‘buy one, get one free’, (11) which persuade shoppers to buy extra items that they may never use. (12) For example, a family might buy two bags of salad because of a discount and then throw one away a week later. This is especially common with fresh food like fruit and bread, which only lasts a few days. A second cause is confusion about date labels: many people throw food away (13) as soon as the date on the packet has passed, even if it is still safe to eat.

However, there are several ways to solve this problem. Firstly, families could plan their meals for the week and write a shopping list, so that they (14) buy only what they need. Secondly, supermarkets could be required to give unsold food to charities (15) instead of throwing it away. (16) As a result, less food would be wasted, and people in need would benefit (17) from it. Finally, governments could run campaigns to explain the (18) difference between ‘best before’ and ‘use by’ dates, and schools could teach children simple ways to store food and cook with leftovers.

In conclusion, food waste is mainly (19) caused by buying too much and by confusion about labels. However, if families plan more carefully (20) and supermarkets donate unsold food, this problem can be greatly reduced.

  • ✔ It answers both parts of the question: the causes (paragraph 2) and the solutions (paragraph 3).

  • ✔ A good range of linking words: such as, For example, A second cause, Firstly, Secondly, As a result, Finally, However.
  • ✔ Complex sentences: …, which persuade shoppers to…; if families plan more carefully…, this problem can be greatly reduced.
  • ✘ Some ideas could be developed further, and the vocabulary is good but quite common.

Although food is a basic necessity, a striking amount of it is thrown away by households, shops and restaurants, wasting money and adding to the pressure on the environment. In my view, this waste stems (9) mainly from consumer habits and confusing date labels, but it could be significantly reduced through a combination of education and regulation.

The most significant cause lies in the way people shop. Large weekly shops and bulk discounts encourage consumers to buy more perishable food than they can realistically eat, and much of it is (10) discarded before it is ever used. Busy lifestyles make matters worse: plans to cook at home are often abandoned in favour of takeaways, leaving fresh ingredients to spoil in the fridge. (11) Moreover, date labels are widely (12) misunderstood: many shoppers treat a ‘best before’ date, which relates to quality, as if it were a safety deadline, and throw away food that is perfectly (13) safe to eat.

(14) Nevertheless, there are effective ways to tackle the problem. Governments could require supermarkets to donate unsold food to charities, as some countries have already done, (15) ensuring that surplus food reaches people in need rather than landfill. At the same time, public (16) awareness campaigns could explain the difference between ‘best before’ and ‘use by’ dates, so that consumers learn to trust their own judgement rather than the label alone. If such measures (17) were introduced, households would waste less food and (18) save money in the process.

In conclusion, food waste is largely a (19) product of shopping habits and misleading labels. With clearer information and sensible regulation, it could be reduced (20) considerably, benefiting both households and the environment.

Why this is a Band 7 answer

  • ✔ A clear position in the introduction: two causes and two kinds of solution are announced, then developed.
  • ✔ The causes and the solutions are linked: shopping habits ↔ donating unsold food; confusing labels ↔ awareness campaigns.
  • ✔ Precise, less common vocabulary: stems from, perishable, bulk discounts, surplus food, landfill, sensible regulation.
  • ✔ A range of complex structures: a relative clause (which relates to quality), as if it were, the second conditional (If such measures were introduced…), a participle clause (…, ensuring that…).
  • To reach Band 8: add a specific example from experience to each body paragraph and keep this accuracy all the way through.

Before that, we’d only ever said hello in the corridor, but now we’re really close — she even taught me how to make her famous spring rolls. I felt proud that I’d been able to help, and it reminded me that small actions can make a big difference.

Follow-up question: Do you still see Mrs Lan?
Yes, all the time — I usually pop round for a cup of tea at the weekend, and she’s still teaching me to cook.

W4 Speaking · Challenging (Band 7–7.5)
QAnswerWhy
1We had been driving for hours when the car suddenly broke down.

Past perfect continuous (had been driving) for a long action up to a past moment, and the past simple (broke down) for the interruption.

2I’d like to talk about my grandmother, who’s probably the person I admire most.

A natural opener that introduces the topic in your own words. describe takes no about (describe my grandmother), and the second option says the same thing twice.

3It taught me something surprising.

an eye-opener = an experience that shows you something new or surprising. It is about what you learn, not about what you see.

4It’s on the tip of my tongue… a big umbrella over a table outside — a parasol!

It’s on the tip of my tongue + a paraphrase keeps you fluent. Skipping the idea or apologising only draws attention to the problem.

5What struck me most was how calm everyone stayed.

A cleft sentence (What struck me most was…) puts the focus on your key idea. The thing what → The thing that.

6exhausted

ex·haust·ed (after t → /ɪd/). relieved and amazed end in /d/ and keep the same number of syllables.

7In hindsight, it was a turning point: organising it gave me the confidence to apply for my current job.

Reflection (In hindsight), a precise phrase (a turning point) and a real consequence. The first answer only describes the event; the second gives no real reason (special, meaningful).

8unforgettable

un·for·GET·ta·ble. MEM·o·ra·ble and COMF·ta·ble are stressed on the first syllable.

9Now and then, yes — it always comes up when someone plans a party, and we end up laughing.

Part 2 follow-up questions are short and about you: answer briefly and personally, with a detail (Now and then… it always comes up when…). The first answer just repeats experience; the third talks about people in general — that is Part 3 style.

10The market was buzzing — stalls piled high with mangoes, and the smell of grilled pork everywhere.

Specific nouns (mangoes, grilled pork), a strong verb (buzzing) and the senses (the smell of…) make a story come alive. The other two are correct but general (busy, interesting, all kinds of things).

11I wish I had taken more photos that day.

Regret about the past: wish + past perfect (I wish I had taken…).

12about 3–4 minutes

1 minute to prepare + up to 2 minutes of talking + one or two short questions = about 3–4 minutes.

Now practise aloud: sample answers

Cue card: Describe an event that did not go as planned. You should say: what the event was · what you had planned · what went wrong · and explain how you felt about it.
1-minute notes: best friend’s surprise birthday picnic · Vũng Tàu beach · weeks of plans: minivan, cake, playlist · storm → cake ruined, soaked · tiny seafood restaurant, owner lent towels · “the rain party” — better than the plan
I’d like to describe my best friend’s birthday last year, which turned out very differently from what we’d planned. A group of us had decided to throw her a surprise picnic on the beach in Vũng Tàu, so we’d spent weeks organising everything — we’d booked a minivan, ordered a cake and even made a playlist of her favourite songs. The plan was to set everything up at sunset and then bring her down to the beach with her eyes covered. Unfortunately, the weather had other ideas. We’d been setting up for about twenty minutes when the sky suddenly turned black, and within seconds it was pouring with rain. The cake was ruined, the decorations blew away, and we were all soaked to the skin. For a moment, I honestly thought the whole thing was a disaster. But then something unexpected happened. We ran into a tiny seafood restaurant nearby, and the owner, who’d obviously seen everything, gave us a corner table and lent us some towels. We ended up spending the whole evening there, eating grilled squid and singing along to the playlist on someone’s phone. When my friend finally arrived, still with her eyes covered and very confused, she burst out laughing. Looking back, the thing I find most surprising is that the evening was far more memorable than the party we’d planned. It taught me that you can’t control everything, and that some of the best moments come from things going wrong. We still joke about “the rain party” whenever we meet.

Follow-up question: Would you organise a surprise party again?
Definitely — but next time I’d check the weather forecast first and have a back-up plan, just in case!

MOCK EXAM 1 · BAND 5–6

Mock Exam 1 — start here

A full IELTS Academic test: Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking

This is your first full practice test. It has the same four parts as the real IELTS Academic test, at Band 5–6 level. Take it like a real exam: it shows you where you are now and what to work on next. Bài thi thử đầu tiên — hãy làm như thi thật!

The four tests — do them in this order
#TestWhat you doTime limit
1 Listening
Mock Exam 1 · Listening (Band 5–6)		4 recordings (about 26 minutes) · 40 questions. Play each recording once and type your answers while you listen; use the time at the end to check them.40 minutes
2 Reading
Mock Exam 1 · Reading (Band 5–6)		3 passages · 40 questions. Spend about 20 minutes on each passage.60 minutes
3 Writing
Mock Exam 1 · Writing (Band 5–6)		Write Task 1 (about 20 minutes, 150+ words) and Task 2 (about 40 minutes, 250+ words) on paper, then answer 20 questions about the tasks (about 20 minutes).80 minutes
4 Speaking
Mock Exam 1 · Speaking (Band 5–6)		About 12 minutes speaking aloud (Parts 1, 2 and 3 — record yourself if you can), then 15 questions.25 minutes

Rules — like the real test

  • Do all four tests in one sitting if you can (Listening → Reading → Writing → Speaking: about 3½ hours with short breaks), as in the real exam. If you cannot, do each test in one go.
  • Use headphones in a quiet room, and play each recording once only, without pausing or going back — in the real test you hear it once.
  • No dictionary, translator, notes or help from other people. Write your Writing answers by hand on paper, or in a document with the spell check turned off.
  • Typed answers: capital letters do not matter, but spelling does. Keep to the word limit in each instruction.
Your Listening and Reading band

To turn your Listening and Reading marks (out of 40) into an IELTS band, use the official figures:

Band scoreListening: marks out of 40Academic Reading: marks out of 40
Band 51615

Source: IELTS, “IELTS scoring in detail” — ielts.org (checked 27 Oct 2026). “The precise number of marks needed to achieve these band scores will vary slightly from test version to test version.” If your mark is between two rows, your band is between those two bands — for example, 26 out of 40 in Listening is about Band 6 to 6.5. There is no band for Writing and Speaking in this mock: use the model answers and the self-check list instead.

Reviewing your answers
  • Listening and Reading: look at every mistake. Was it spelling, the word limit, a trap — or did you not hear or find the answer? Listen again and read the transcript at the same time.
  • Writing: compare your two answers with the model answers and go through the self-check list.
  • Speaking: read the model answers aloud, then answer the questions again and record yourself.
